<term>Grahashanti</term>: Rituals performed in Hindu tradition to pacify or harmonize the influences of the nine celestial bodies (planets) in a person's horoscope.

<term>Paddhati</term>: A systematic step-by-step manual or "how-to" guide for performing a specific ritual.

<term>Shivdatti</term>: The title of the explanatory commentary accompanying the original Sanskrit verses.

<term>Hindi-teeka</term>: A commentary or translation provided in the Hindi language to make the text accessible to those who may not be fluent in Sanskrit.

<term>Acharya</term>: A scholar who has mastered the sacred scriptures and teaches them to others.

<term>Varanasi</term>: A city in northern India famous for its spiritual significance and as a hub for traditional Sanskrit education.

<term>Prakashak</term>: The individual or company responsible for publishing the work.

In this book, the presentation of all the worship rituals that form an integral part of Vedic sacrifices and offerings is available in a simple and accessible method. It is certain that this will contribute to the growth and propagation of Indian culture.

In this work, along with the original Sanskrit text, the sequence of various rituals is beautifully described in simple Hindi—a feature that is unavailable in other books. With the help of this manual, even an ordinary <term>Karmakandi</term> <note>A priest specializing in the ritual procedures of the Vedas.</note> will be able to perform his duties excellently; this is also certain. This labor of yours is entirely praiseworthy.

<header>Preface</header>
<margin>Grahashanti Paddhati, Page 5</margin>

# Preface

For practitioners of sacred rituals <note>karmakandis</note>, the "Method of Planetary Pacification" <note>Grahashanti-paddhati</note> holds a primary position. In all rites performed for peace <note>shantikarma</note> and various Vedic sacrifices <note>yajna-yagadi</note>, the pacification of the planets is mandatorily prescribed by the scriptures <note>shastras</note> and is indeed essential. As it has been said:

> ->The planets bestow kingdoms, and the planets take them away.<-
> ->This entire universe, containing all things moving and unmoving, is pervaded by the planets.<-
<note>original Sanskrit: "ग्रहा राज्यं प्रयच्छन्ति ग्रहा राज्यं हरन्ति च । ग्रहे व्याप्तमिदं सर्वं त्रैलोक्यं सचराचरम् ॥"</note>

That is to say, auspicious planets are helpful in granting sovereign power to rulers, whereas malefic planets can destroy a king's domain. The entire world, consisting of both sentient and insentient beings, is influenced by these planetary forces. Furthermore:

> ->Planets, cows, kings, and especially the <term>Brahmins</term>;<-
> ->When honored, these bring prosperity; when insulted, they consume with fire.<-
<note>original Sanskrit: "ग्रहा गावो नरेन्द्राश्च ब्राह्मणाश्च विशेषतः । पूजिताः पूजयन्त्येते निर्दहन्त्यपमानिताः ॥"</note>

Meaning that the planets, cows, kings, and particularly the <term>Brahmins</term> <note>the priestly and scholarly class</note> grant progress when they are honored within the three worlds. However, if they are insulted or ignored, they can bring about total destruction.

The core meaning is that for human beings, performing pacification rituals according to the prescribed rules <term>sa-vidhi</term> is absolutely necessary to ensure the favor of the planets. For this purpose, the present "Method of Planetary Pacification" is entirely useful and significant.

Although other versions of planetary pacification manuals have been published, this present method is entirely innovative in its style—simple, easy to follow, and accessible even to general scholars.

**Key Terminology:**
<term>Karmakanda</term> (the section of the Vedas related to ceremonial rituals), <term>Grahashanti-paddhati</term> (a manual for planetary pacification), <term>Shantikarma</term> (rituals performed to avert evil or bring peace), <term>Yajna-Yagadi</term> (various types of fire sacrifices), <term>Shastra</term> (sacred scriptures or systematic treatises), <term>Graha</term> (celestial bodies or "seizers" that influence human fate), <term>Trailokya</term> (the three worlds: heaven, earth, and the underworld), <term>Brahmin</term> (the scholarly and priestly class), <term>Sa-vidhi</term> (performing an act exactly as prescribed by ritual law).

<summary>This preface explains the vital importance of planetary pacification rituals in Vedic life, asserting that planets control the rise and fall of kingdoms and the well-being of all creatures.</summary>
<keywords>astrology, planetary pacification, Grahashanti, ritual importance, Vedic scriptures, Brahmins, karma, cosmic influence</keywords>

<margin>Preface</margin>

Included here—along with a Hindi commentary—are the procedure for Planetary Pacification <note>Grahashanti</note>, the Auspicious Benediction <note>Swastivachan</note>, the worship of Ganesha and Ambika, the installation and worship of the Sacred Pot <note>Kalash</note>, the Declaration of a Sanctified Day <note>Punyahavachan</note>, the Worship for the Removal of Obstacles <note>Avighna Pujan</note>, the installation and consecration of the Ritual Pavilion <note>Mandap</note>, the worship of the Sixteen Mother Goddesses <note>Shodash Matrika</note>, the "Flow of Wealth" ritual <note>Vasordhara Pujan; a ritual involving the pouring of ghee</note>, the chanting of Mantras for Longevity <note>Ayushya Mantra</note>, the Ancestral Offerings for Auspicious Occasions <note>Nandi-Shraddha</note>, and many other subjects. It also includes the correct installation and worship of all the deities within the "Auspicious from All Sides" <note>Sarvatobhadra</note> and "Auspicious from the Linga" <note>Lingatobhadra</note> sacred mandalas.

The creation of this methodology in a simple and accessible style with a Hindi commentary, along with the inclusion of an index of Mantras and an index of Verses, are the primary features of this book—features which are generally unavailable in the methodologies published until now. Through this present methodology, even ordinary scholars can properly conduct all Vedic sacraments <note>Samskaras</note>, rituals for peace <note>Shantikarma</note>, and various Vedic sacrifices <note>Yajna-yagadi</note>. There is no doubt that by completely memorizing this, every <term>Brahmin</term> <note>priest</note> can fearlessly and without hesitation recite the Vedic mantras in all sacrificial rituals.

I express my special gratitude to the Sovereign of the Kashi Seat <note>Kashi Pithadhishwar</note>, the infinite and divinely adorned, the venerable Jagadguru Shankaracharya—Swami Shri Shankarananda Saraswati Ji Maharaj, who, despite his extremely busy schedule, showed me immense compassion and graced this text by providing his best wishes for this book. I offer my heartfelt blessings to the young Shri Punit Kumar Sharma, who worked with great diligence on the task of creating the indices for the mantras and verses, as well as on the proofreading.

---

Shravani Purnima <note>The full moon day of the month of Shravan, a traditional day for scholars to renew their studies</note>  
11 August 1964

->—Shivadatta Mishra Shastri<-  
->C.K. 5/26 A.<-  
->Bhikhari Das Lane, Varanasi-1<-

# The System of Planetary Peace

### Accompanied by the ‘Shivadatti’ Hindi Commentary

->Auspicious Invocation<-
<note>original: "Mangalacharanam"; a traditional opening prayer intended to bring divine favor to the author and the reader.</note>

> I bow to my father, Santasharana, and likewise to my mother, Jayanti; and I eternally bow to the venerable Lord Ganesha, the giver of all auspiciousness. || 1 ||
>
> Having extracted the essence of the scriptures for the great joy of the learned, Shivadatta Mishra now expands upon the <term>System of Planetary Peace</term> <note>original: "Grahashanti-paddhati"; a "paddhati" is a manual or step-by-step guide for performing specific Vedic rituals, in this case, rituals to appease the nine planets (Grahas) in Hindu astrology.</note>. || 2 ||

---

I bow to my father Santasharana, my mother Jayanti, and to the venerable Lord Ganesha, who is the eternal bestower of all that is auspicious. || 1 ||

Having bathed thoroughly and facing the East, the <term>patron</term> <note>original: "Yajamana"; the person who sponsors and benefits from the religious ceremony</note>, having completed his daily morning prayers, should summon the <term>priests</term> <note>original: "Brahmins"</note> and then formally state his vow <note>original: "Pratijna"; a formal declaration of intent to perform the ritual for a specific purpose</note> according to the prescribed rules. || 1 ||

After performing the worship of <term>Ganesha</term> and then <term>Varuna</term> <note>Varuna is the Vedic deity of the waters, typically worshiped here via a consecrated water pot or Kalasha</note>, and carrying out the ‘Declaration of an Auspicious Day,’ he should then have the ritual consecration performed by the priests. || 2 ||

---

**The order of the Ritual for Planetary Peace—**

The patron, after having bathed well and being free from his daily chores, should call the priests and obtain their permission by stating: “I wish to perform the Ritual for Planetary Peace for such-and-such a purpose.” || 1 || 

First of all, he should worship <term>Ganesha</term> and <term>Ambika</term> <note>Ambika is a form of the Mother Goddess, often worshiped alongside Ganesha at the start of rituals</note>, establish the sacred water pot <note>original: "Kalasha-sthapana"</note>, perform the <term>Declaration of an Auspicious Day</term> <note>original: "Punyahavachanam"; a rite to ensure the time and environment are spiritually pure</note>, and then have the <term>consecration</term> <note>original: "Abhisheka"; a ritual bathing or sprinkling of sanctified water</note> performed by the priests. || 2 ||

Perform the fire sacrifice for the deities. Also, worship the Sacred Fire, and perform the <term>Svishtakrit</term> <note>the concluding portion of a fire sacrifice where a final offering is made to Agni to ensure the ritual's success</note> oblation using the remaining ritual mixture <note>original: "shakala"</note> all at once, then offer nine final oblations consisting only of clarified butter. || 7 ||

After that, present food offerings <note>original: "bali"</note> along with lamps for the Guardians of the Directions. After giving the food offerings for the Sun and the other planets, and the offering for the presiding deity, give the offering for the <term>Kshetrapala</term> <note>the protective deity or "Guardian of the Field" associated with the specific land</note>. || 8 ||

Thereafter, perform the <term>Purnahuti</term> <note>the "Full Offering" marking the completion of the fire ritual</note> and then the <term>Vasoddhara</term> <note>the "Stream of Wealth" offering</note>. Taking sacred ash from the altar with the ritual spoon, and after performing the "Triple-Life" blessing, carry out the ritual sipping of the remains and other concluding acts. || 9 ||

Again, receive blessings from the Brahmins and, after giving them a ritual fee of gold, have the consecration and other rites performed. Finally, sprinkle <term>akshata</term> <note>unbroken ritual rice grains</note> upon the installed deities and perform the formal dismissal. These are the actions required in the ritual for planetary peace. || 10 ||

# Ritual Procedure:

At a time when the auspicious planets are favorable, on an auspicious day and during an auspicious astrological sign (<term>lagna</term> <note>the specific zodiac sign rising on the eastern horizon at the time of the ritual</note>), the patron (<term>yajamana</term> <note>the person who sponsors and benefits from the ritual</note>), having completed his daily morning rites, should sit on a sacred seat facing East. He should seat his wife to his right <gloss>1</gloss>. He then sips water three times (<term>achamana</term> <note>a ritual purification where water is sipped from the palm to cleanse the speech and body</note>) while reciting: **"Om, salutations to Keshava; Om, salutations to Narayana; Om, salutations to Madhava."**

> **Om, you two are the purifiers, sacred to Vishnu. May the Creator purify you; I purify you with the flawless purifier, the rays of the Sun. O Lord of Purifiers, through you, purified by that which is already pure, may I be able to attain that which I desire.**
<note>original: "pavitre stho vaishnavyau..." This Vedic mantra is recited while handling the *pavitra*—two blades of sacred grass used to symbolically filter and purify the ritual ingredients.</note>

---

The patron should perform the twilight prayers and other daily duties. Then, at an auspicious planetary time, day, and astrological sign, he should sit on a seat made of sacred <term>kusha</term> grass facing East. He should then sip water three times while saying "Om, salutations to Keshava; Om, salutations to Narayana; Om, salutations to Madhava."

---

1. The person undergoing the sacrament—whether a man or a woman—should always sit to the right. The person performing the sacrament (the priest) should always stand to the north. — Thus it is stated in the *Prayogaparijata* <note>The "Coral Tree of Ritual Procedure," a classic medieval handbook for Hindu domestic rites</note>.

<summary>This page describes the preparatory purification rites for a Hindu ritual, focusing on the timing, seating of the patron and his wife, and the initial sipping of water (Achamana).</summary>
<keywords>ritual procedure, achamana, purification, yajamana, astrological timing, Prayogaparijata, sacred grass</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the ritual instructions from page 6. Having seated himself and performed the initial sips of water, the practitioner now moves into active purification of the body and the ritual space, followed by the symbolic creation of the primary deities on the altar.</meta>

<page-num>7</page-num>
<header>Planetary Section, Page 7</header>
<header>Procedure 7</header>

Having worn the sacred purifier (<term>pavitra</term> <note>original: "pavitra-dharanam"; a ceremonial ring or filter woven from blades of kusha grass</note>) made of <term>kusha</term> grass and other materials while reciting the previously mentioned mantra, one should then perform three rounds of breath control (<term>pranayama</term>).

->**Om, whether one is impure or pure, or has passed through any state of being,**<-
->**he who remembers the Lotus-Eyed Lord <note>Pundarikaksha, an epithet of the god Vishnu</note> becomes pure both outwardly and inwardly.**<-

"Om, may the Lotus-Eyed Lord purify me" (recite three times). With this, one should sprinkle water upon oneself and the worship materials (<term>puja-samagri</term> <note>the various items used in the ritual, such as flowers, incense, and offerings</note>).

Then, on a copper or earthen vessel filled with rice, draw an eight-petaled lotus using red saffron powder (<term>kumkum</term>). Upon this, establish the goddess Gauri represented by cow dung <note>cow dung is considered highly purifying in Hindu ritual and is often used to mold a small symbolic form of the Goddess</note> and the god Ganesha represented by a fruit <note>original: "phalamayam"; usually a betel nut is used to symbolize Ganesha</note>.

---

Then, reciting the mantras from "Om, you two are the purifiers" <note>original: "Om pavitre stho"</note> to "attain that which I desire" <note>original: "tachhakeyam"</note>, wear the grass purifier and perform breath control three times. Reciting from "Om, whether one is impure or pure" to "may the Lotus-Eyed Lord purify me," sprinkle water upon yourself and the ritual materials.

After that, on an earthen or copper vessel filled with rice, create an eight-petaled lotus using red powder (<term>rori</term>). Upon it, establish Gauri made of cow dung and Ganesha upon a betel nut.

# The Auspicious Invocation

The patron of the ritual <term>yajamana</term> <note>original: "yajamana"; the person sponsoring and benefiting from the religious service</note>, taking unbroken rice grains <term>akshata</term> <note>original: "akshata"; literally "unbroken," these are rice grains colored with turmeric or vermilion used as a sacred offering</note> and flowers in the right hand, should recite the mantras of the Auspicious Invocation (<term>Svasti-vachana</term>) beginning with "May noble thoughts..." <note>original: "Aa no bhadra"</note> and so on. They are as follows:

> Om. May noble thoughts come to us from every side, unhindered, unabated, and all-pervading.
> May the gods be with us always for our growth, our protectors who never fail us, day by day. (1)
> May the auspicious favor of the gods—who are straightforward and upright—be directed toward us. May the generosity of the gods turn toward us. May the friendship of the gods <note>The original text contains a specific Vedic phonetic marker indicating a nasalized "gum" sound for the preceding syllable</note>—

---

**Auspicious Invocation**—The patron, taking unbroken rice and flowers in the right hand, should recite the mantras from "Om, may noble thoughts" <note>original: "Om aa no bhadrah"</note> through "May there be perfect peace" <note>original: "su-shantir-bhavatu"</note>, as well as the naming prayers from "Salutations to the Great Lord of the Ganas" <note>original: "Shri-man-maha-ganadhipataye namah"</note> through "Brahma, Shiva, and Vishnu" <note>original: "Brahmeshaana-janardanaah"</note>. Having completed the recitation, he should drop the rice and flowers upon the symbols representing Ganesha and Gauri.

<summary>This page contains the opening of the Svasti Vacana, a traditional Vedic ceremony of benediction. It instructs the patron to hold sacred rice and flowers while chanting hymns from the Rigveda to ensure the ritual's success and the presence of the gods.</summary>
<keywords>Svasti Vacana, Auspicious Invocation, Rigveda, Yajamana, Ganesha, Gauri, ritual procedure, Vedic mantras</keywords>

<term>अनन्यांश्चिन्तयन्तः (Ananyāṃś-cintayantaḥ)</term>: Literally "thinking of no other." It refers to single-minded devotion where the seeker sees the divine in everything.

<term>स्वस्तिवाचनम् (Svasti-vacanam)</term>: A preliminary rite in Hindu rituals where priests or practitioners recite specific Vedic or Puranic verses to invoke "Svasti" (well-being, peace, and prosperity) before the main ceremony begins.

<term>ब्रह्मेशान-जनार्दना: (Brahma-Īśāna-Janārdanāḥ)</term>: A compound referring to the Hindu Trinity: Brahma (the Creator), Ishana (a name for Shiva, the Transformer), and Janardana (a name for Vishnu, the Preserver). Calling upon all three signifies a total harmony of cosmic forces.

### The Resolution <note>original: "Sankalpa"</note>—The patron <note>the person for whom the ritual is performed</note> should take water, unbroken rice grains <note>original: "akshata"</note>, and ritual offerings <note>usually coins or sacrificial materials</note> and make the resolution as follows:

Vishnu, Vishnu, Vishnu! <note>The name of the Preserver is repeated thrice to sanctify the air and the mind.</note> By the command of the Blessed Lord, the Supreme Person Vishnu, which is now in effect: Today, in the second half of the life-cycle of Lord Brahma <note>the creator god's life is used as the largest unit of cosmic time</note>, in the "Step of Vishnu," in the Aeon of the White Boar <note>original: "Shveta-Varaha-Kalpa"</note>, in the era of the Sun-born Progenitor <note>original: "Vaivasvata-manvantare"</note>, in the twenty-eighth cycle of ages, in the Age of Discord <note>original: "Kaliyuga"</note>, in the first quarter of that age, in the realm of the Earth, in the Continent of the Rose-Apple Tree <note>original: "Jambu-dvipa"</note>, in the Land of Bharat, in the region of Bharat, in a certain part of the Land of the Noble Ones <note>original: "Aryavarta"</note> (specifically at the Sacred Site of the Unforsaken Varanasi <note>Kashi</note>, in the Forest of Bliss, in the Great Cremation Ground, at the Face of Gauri, resplendent with the Trident of Shiva <note>the "Three Spokes"</note>, on the western bank of the Ganges), in the era of King Vikrama, during the incarnation of the Buddha, in the year named [Blank] <note>original: "amuka"; ---

The Resolution—The patron, taking water, rice grains, and ritual offerings in the right hand, recites from "Om, Vishnu, Vishnu, Vishnu" until the phrase "I shall perform the pacification of the planets." <note>original: "graha-shantim-aham karishye"</note>

<term>सङ्कल्प (Sankalpa)</term>: A solemn vow or declaration of intent made at the start of a ritual. It acts as a "spiritual contract" that links the specific time, place, and person to the divine act.

<term>जम्बुद्वीप (Jambu-dvipa)</term>: "The Island of the Rose-Apple Tree." In ancient Hindu cosmology, this is the central continent of the world where humans live.

<term>अविमुक्तवाराणसीक्षेत्र (Avimukta-Varanasi-kshetra)</term>: "The region of Varanasi that is never forsaken [by Shiva]." This is a highly poetic and sacred way of identifying the city of Benares.

<header>Ganesha Worship, Page 16</header>

# The Worship of Ganesha and Ambika

Taking unbroken grains of rice in the hand, one should invite Lord Ganesha and worship him with the **sixteen-fold offerings** <term>Shodashopachara|The traditional sixteen steps of hospitality offered to a deity, treating them as an honored guest</term>. The meditation is as follows:

## One should meditate upon the god who has a single tusk, ears like winnowing baskets, an elephant’s face, and four arms.
## Holding a noose and a goad, he is the Lord who grants success and removes obstacles. ||1||

## One should meditate upon the elephant-faced god, who possesses a brilliance like molten gold.
## He has four arms, a massive body, and is adorned with every kind of ornament. ||2||

---

**The Invocation for the Worship of Ganesha and Ambika**—Taking unbroken rice grains <term>Akshata|Whole, unpolished rice grains used in ritual to symbolize abundance and permanence</term> in the right hand, recite the verses starting from "One with a single tusk..." up to "Protect my worship and sacrifice," as well as the Vedic mantra "Om, we invoke you, the Lord of the Ganas..." <note>original: "Om gananam tva..."—a famous verse from the Rig Veda (2.23.1) used to invoke Ganesha</note> ending with "I establish you." Then, release the rice and flowers onto the image of Ganesha.

---

1. The sixteen-fold offerings are described in the *Karmapradipa* <note>A classical Sanskrit text detailing the "Lamp of Ritual Action"</note>: "Invocation, offering a seat, water for washing the feet, water for the hands, and water for sipping. Bathing, offering garments and the sacred thread, and then applying fragrance and flower garlands in sequence. ||1||
> Incense, a lamp, an offering of food, betel nut with spices, and circumambulation. The offering of a handful of flowers completes what are known as the sixteen steps of worship. ||2||
> 'Through the offering of fruit, the full fruit of the ritual is obtained; through the offering of the priest’s fee <term>Dakshina|A ritual gift or honorarium that validates the sacrifice</term>, the ceremony is made complete in all its parts.'"

<vocab>Worship of Ganesha and Ambika, Sixteen-fold offerings, Invocation, Lamp of Ritual Action, Elephant-faced god, Lord of Success, Unbroken rice</vocab>

<summary>This page details the initial invocation and meditation on Lord Ganesha, outlining the sixteen standard steps of ritual worship used to honor the deity at the start of the ceremony.</summary>
<keywords>Ganesha, Ambika, meditation verses, Shodashopachara, ritual offerings, Hindu liturgy, Karmapradipa</keywords>

### Ritual Instructions

**Honorific Water (Arghya):** After reciting from "Salutations to the Leader of the Hosts" <note>referencing the verse from the previous page</note> until "I offer the honorific water," offer the Arghya to Ganesha and Gauri <note>Gauri is another name for the goddess Ambika</note>.

**Ritual Sipping (Achamana):** After reciting from "Salutations to you, O Vinayaka" until "I offer the ritual sipping water," release one spoonful <term>Achamani|A small copper or silver spoon used specifically for dispensing ritual water</term> of water into the offering bowl.

Om! You waters are indeed the source of bliss; help us by granting us strength, so that we may behold great and beautiful joy. <note>original: "oṃ āpo hi ṣṭhā mayobhuvastā na ūrdje dadhātana | mahe raṇāya cakṣase ||" — This is a famous Vedic hymn (Rigveda 10.9.1) used for purification. It asks the water to nourish the worshiper like a loving mother.</note> (Alternatively) Those with white tails, those with entirely white tails, and those with jewel-like tails are for the <term>Ashvins</term> <note>The Ashvins are the twin divine physicians of the gods.</note>; the white ones, those with white eyes, and the reddish ones are for <term>Rudra</term> in his form as the Lord of Animals; the long-eared ones are for <term>Yama</term> <note>The god of death and justice.</note>; those smeared with color are for the Storm Gods; those the color of the sky are for the Rain God. <note>original: "śuddhavālaḥ sarvaśuddhavālo... pārjanyāḥ ||" — This verse from the Shukla Yajurveda (24.3) lists specific sacrificial animals and their associated deities. In this ritual context, the recitation serves to invoke the totality of the divine pantheon to sanctify the water.</note>

->**The Ganges, the Yamuna, the Godavari, and the Saraswati;**<-
->**the Narmada, the Indus, and the Kaveri—please accept these waters for the purpose of the ritual bath.** <note>original: "gaṅgā ca yamunā caiva godāvarī sarasvatī | narmadā sindhu kāverī snānārthaṃ pratigṛhyatām ||" — Known as the Sapta Sindhu mantra, this verse is recited to mentally summon the seven holiest rivers of India into the water pot, making the bath spiritually equivalent to a pilgrimage.</note><-

<summary>This page concludes the ritual bathing (Abhisheka) of the deities by providing the Vedic and Puranic mantras for the final pure water bath. It invokes the healing power of water and the spiritual presence of the seven sacred rivers of India.</summary>

<vocab>
**Anointment** (Vilepana): the act of applying paste or oil to a deity.
**Best of gods** (Surashreshtha): an epithet used for Ganesha or the primary deity being worshipped.
**Sandalwood** (Chandana): a fragrant wood used as a paste in Hindu rituals.
**Gandharvas**: divine beings in Vedic mythology known for their knowledge of medicinal and sacred plants.
**Consumption** (Yakshma): a term for illness, often used in Vedic hymns as something the gods and herbs can banish.
**Ganesha and Ambika**: the two deities being worshipped; Ganesha is the remover of obstacles and Ambika (Gauri) is the Mother Goddess.
**Unbroken rice** (Akshata): whole grains of rice, usually dyed with turmeric or vermilion, used as an offering.
**Anointed with vermilion** (Kumkumakta): rice grains covered in *kumkuma*, a sacred red powder.
**Supreme Lord** (Parameshvara): a title for the highest divinity.
</vocab>

<term>Ganeshambika (Ganesha-Ambika)</term>: The joint invocation of the elephant-headed god Ganesha and the Mother Goddess Ambika (or Gauri), who are traditionally worshipped first in Hindu rituals to ensure success and auspiciousness.
<term>Dhupa (Incense)</term>: A sensory offering representing the element of Air, intended to purify the atmosphere and please the deity with fragrance.
<term>Deepa (Lamp)</term>: An offering representing the element of Fire and the light of knowledge, used to illuminate the deity and remove spiritual ignorance.

<summary>This page details the specific Sanskrit mantras and ritual instructions for offering incense and a ceremonial lamp to Ganesha and Ambika, emphasizing the removal of darkness and spiritual protection.</summary>
<keywords>incense offering, lamp ritual, Ganesha, Ambika, Vedic mantras, light vs darkness, ghee lamp, Hindu liturgy</keywords>

# Om! Agni is light, light is Agni, hail! Surya is light, light is Surya, hail!
<note>original: "agnirjyotirjyotiragniḥ svāhā sūryo jyotirjyotiḥ sūryyaḥ svāhā" — These are traditional Agnihotra mantras. 'Svaha' is an exclamation used when pouring offerings into the consecrated fire. The mantra identifies Agni (the ritual fire) with Surya (the Sun), symbolizing that the earthly flame and the celestial sun are manifestations of the same divine light.</note>

->**Om! From His navel the atmosphere arose; from His head the sky evolved.**<-
<note>original: "oṃ nābhyā āsīdantarikṣaṃ śīrṣṇo dyauḥ samavarttata" — This is a verse from the *Purusha Sukta* (Rig Veda 10.90.14), the "Hymn of the Cosmic Man." By reciting this, the priest acknowledges that the food being offered is part of the same cosmic cycle of creation.</note>

<margin>Special Libation</margin>
Having placed water, sandalwood paste, <term>akshata: unbroken, consecrated grains of rice</term>, fruit, flowers, <term>durva: a sacred grass used in Hindu rituals for its purifying properties</term>, and <term>dakshina: a small monetary offering</term> in a copper vessel or a clay pot, hold that libation vessel in the palms of both hands. Recite the prayers starting from "Protect, protect" down to "I offer this special libation," and then pour the libation water from that vessel onto the images of <term>Gauri-Ganapati: the Mother Goddess Gauri and the god Ganesha</term>.

<margin>Planet Rituals p. 58 <note>original: "graha pa 58"</note></margin> **Installation and Worship of the Pot** — The <term>Yajamana: the patron of the ritual</term> should place a pile of rice on a leaf-plate. Upon these, he should draw an eight-petaled lotus using <term>Rori: a red powder used for sacred markings</term>. Reciting the mantras from "Om. May the great Sky..." <note>original: "oṃ mahī dyauḥ"</note> to "with sustaining powers," <note>original: "bharīmabhiḥ"</note> he should touch that leaf-plate situated on the ground.

Then, reciting the mantra from "Om. The medicinal herbs spoke together..." <note>original: "oṃ oṣadhayaḥ saṃvadanta"</note> to "we carry across," <note>original: "pārayāmasi"</note> he should establish the <term>Saptadhanya: a mixture of seven sacred grains</term> upon the leaf-plate. Using the mantra "Om. Breathe upon the vessel...", he should then place the <term>Kalasha: the sacred water pot</term> upon the seven grains.

<margin>Ritual Procedures p. 58 <note>original: "ka pū 58"</note></margin> 1. **The Seven Grains** — Barley, wheat, paddy (rice), sesame, millet, as well as barnyard millet and chickpeas are known as the seven grains.
Alternatively — Barley, paddy, sesame, millet, mung beans, chickpeas, and barnyard millet. These seven grains should be employed in all ritual works.

<note>1. **Characteristics of the Purifier:** A ritual purifier (Pavitra) should not include the inner sprout of the grass; it must have its tips intact, be made of Kusha grass, and consist of two blades. It is traditionally measured as one "span" (the distance from the tip of the thumb to the tip of the little finger) in length.</note>
<note>2. **The Seven Earths:** One should collect and deposit soil brought from seven specific locations: a horse stable, an elephant stable, a termite mound, a confluence of rivers, a deep lake, a king's palace gate, and a cow pen.</note>

### Ritual of the Planets; Worship Section; Earlier Actions

After reciting the previous mantra, one should say, "**I invoke <term>Varuna: the ancient Vedic guardian of the cosmic waters and moral law</term> into this vessel, along with his attendants, his retinue, his weapons, and his divine power.**" Then, having said, "**Om. ### The vessel is called a "<term>Kalasha</term>" because it was fashioned by gathering the various portions and powers of the gods and the demons. ||1||
<note>original Sanskrit: "kalākalā hi devānāṃ dānavānāṃ kalākalāḥ | saṅgṛhya nirmito yasmāt kalaśastena kathyate ||" This verse provides an etymological myth for the word 'Kalasha,' deriving it from 'kala' (part or portion).</note>

### Vishnu resides in the mouth of the vessel; Rudra is seated in its neck. Brahma is situated at its base, and the assembly of the Mother Goddesses is remembered as dwelling in its middle. ||2||
<note>original Sanskrit: "kalaśasya mukhe viṣṇuḥ kaṇṭhe rudraḥ samāśritaḥ | mūle tvasya sthito brahmā madhye mātṛgaṇāḥ smṛtāḥ ||" This describes the pot as a microcosm containing the entire Hindu pantheon: the Preserver (Vishnu), the Destroyer (Rudra/Shiva), and the Creator (Brahma).</note>

---

The invocation of the Ganga and other <term>Tirthas: sacred pilgrimage sites or holy watering places</term>—after reading the eight verses starting from "The portions of the gods..." through to "the destroyers of sin," one should pray for the arrival of the Ganga and other sacred rivers into the vessel.

---

<note>1. The five-fold worship consists of: sandalwood paste, flowers, incense, a lamp, and a food offering. The wise person who knows the essential truths should perform these five rituals.</note>

# Prayer to the Sacred Vessel

->The Patron:-- **During the conflict between the gods and the demons, while the great ocean was being churned,**<-

->**You emerged then, O Vessel, and were held by Vishnu himself. || 1 ||**<-
<note>original: "devadanava-samvade" — refers to the famous Vedic myth of the Samudra Manthan or Churning of the Ocean of Milk, where the vessel containing the nectar of immortality (Amrita) emerged.</note>

->**In your waters are all the holy pilgrimage sites; all the gods reside within you.**<-

->**Within you dwell all living beings; in you, the very breaths of life are established. || 2 ||**<-
<note>original: "pranah" — the vital life forces or breaths that sustain a living being.</note>

->**You yourself are Lord Shiva, you are Vishnu, and you are the Lord of Creatures.**<-

->**The Sun-gods, the Elemental-gods, the Storm-gods, and the Universal-gods reside here along with the Ancestors. || 3 ||**<-
<note>The text lists the <term>Adityas: twelve solar deities</term>, the <term>Vasus: eight elemental deities representing aspects of nature</term>, and the <term>Rudras: eleven deities associated with storm and destruction</term>.</note>

---

Having recited this, let him release water onto the ground.

# The Declaration of the Auspicious Day
<note>Sanskrit: <term>Punyahavachanam</term>. This ceremony is performed to ensure the success of a ritual by invoking the collective blessings of the priests and the divine.</note>

The **Yajamana** <note>the patron or host who sponsors the ritual</note>—with both knees touching the ground, placing his cupped hands like a lotus bud upon his head, and then holding the vessel filled with gold (or earth, or copper) with his right hand—should pray for blessings.

---

**Prayer**—Once more, the **Yajamana** should recite the six verses starting from "During the dialogue of the gods and demons" <note>a reference to the beginning of the ritual on previous pages</note> up to "Please remain present here," and pray to the vessel with joined hands. In this manner, the installation and worship of the ritual vessel are concluded.

**The Declaration of the Auspicious Day**—The **Yajamana**, bending his knees to the ground and placing his cupped hands like a lotus flower upon his head, should hold the gold (or clay or copper) vessel and pray for blessings from the priests.

## Long are the serpents, the rivers, the mountains, and the three steps of Vishnu.
## By the measure of their longevity, may there be merit, an auspicious day, and a long life.
<note>original: "Dirgha naga nadyo..." This verse invokes the "long" or eternal nature of geographical and mythological features—serpents (Nagas), rivers, mountains, and Vishnu's strides—as a sympathetic magic to grant the patron a similarly long life.</note>

->**The patron should say this. The priests respond: "Let there be a long life."**<-

## Om. Vishnu, the protector whom none can deceive, strode three steps.
## From there, he upholds the sacred laws. 
<note>original: "Om trini pada vichakrame...". This is a famous Rig Vedic verse (1.22.18) describing Vishnu's Vamana (dwarf) incarnation, where he reclaimed the universe from the demon king Bali in three massive strides. Here, it signifies divine omnipresence and the establishment of <term>Dharma</term> (sacred law).</note>

**Thus the priests should say.**

The **Yajamana** <note>the patron or host of the ritual</note> should say: "By that measure of longevity, may there be merit, an auspicious day, and a long life." The **Twice-born** <note>Sanskrit: <term>Dvija</term>; here referring to the priests</note> respond: "May there be merit, an auspicious day, and a long life." This is repeated twice more over the head...

---

Again, the patron should recite from "Long are the serpents..." until "...may there be a long life."
The Brahmins <note>priests</note> should also say: "Let there be a long life" in this manner. Then the patron should recite from "Om, the three steps..." until "...may there be a long life."

Placing [the vessel] on the ground. **The patron—pouring water into the hands of the Brahmins—should say: "Om, may the waters be auspicious." The Brahmins respond: "May the waters be auspicious." In this manner, they should provide the response after every statement. The patron should offer a flower, saying: "May there be benevolence." The wise ones <note>original: "Viprah," referring to the learned priests</note> respond: "May there be benevolence." The patron should offer unbroken grains <note>Sanskrit: <term>Akshata</term>; unhusked rice grains used in Hindu rituals to symbolize permanence and wholeness</note>, saying: "<gloss>3</gloss>May there be wholeness and freedom from misfortune." The wise ones: "May there be wholeness and freedom from misfortune." The patron should offer fragrance <note>usually sandalwood paste</note>, saying: "May the fragrances protect."**

---

The Brahmins should also say: "May there be merit, an auspicious day, and a long life." In the same way, the patron, after touching the <term>Kalasha</term> <note>a sacred water pot representing the universe and the source of life</note> to his head, shoulders, and knees twice, should place it upon the seven types of grain <note>Sanskrit: <term>Sapta Dhanya</term></note>.

Again, the patron should release water into the hands of the Brahmins, saying: "May the waters be auspicious." The assembly of Brahmins should also say: "May the waters be auspicious."

---

1. The gods reside in the midst of the waters; everything is established in the waters. May these auspicious waters, placed in the hands of the Brahmins, be for your benefit.

2. Lakshmi <note>the goddess of prosperity and beauty</note> resides in flowers; Lakshmi resides in the lotus. May she dwell within me eternally, and likewise, may there be benevolence <note>original: <term>Saumanasyam</term>, implying a peaceful and happy state of mind</note> for us.

3. May my merit be unbroken, and may there be long life, fame, and strength. Whatever is beneficial in this world, may that always be mine.

## Over the Second Vessel:

**"Om. May there be the destruction of misfortune. Om. Whatever sin, disease, misfortune, or ill-omen there be, may it be struck down and driven far away."** 

Inside: 

**"Om. May there be whatever is beneficial. Om. May the subsequent ritual be free of obstacles. Om. May there be growth day by day, higher and higher. Om. May the subsequent actions be auspicious, beautiful, and successful. Om. May there be the abundance of the lunar day, the ritual division, the auspicious moment, the constellation, the planet, and the ascendant.** <note>These terms refer to the *Panchang*, the five limbs of the Hindu calendar used to find the most spiritually potent time for an action.</note> **Om. May the presiding deities of the lunar day, the ritual division, the auspicious moment, the constellation, the planet, and the ascendant be pleased. Om. May the lunar day, the ritual division, the auspicious moment, the constellation, the planet, and the ascendant, together with their presiding deities, be pleased. Om. May the goddesses Durga and Panchali be pleased. Om. May the All-Gods <term>Vishvedevas</term>, led by Agni, be pleased. Om. May the Storm-Gods <term>Maruts</term>, led by Indra, be pleased. Om. May the assembly of Sages, led by Vashistha, be pleased. Om. May the Divine Mothers, led by Maheshwari, be pleased. Om. May the faithful wives, led by Arundhati, be pleased."**

---

And in the second vessel, after reciting from "May there be the destruction of misfortune" until "may it be struck down," one should drop unbroken rice grains <term>Akshata</term>. 
Then, over the water vessel <term>Kalasha</term>, after saying from "May there be whatever is beneficial" until "May the [presiding] deities be pleased," sprinkle the rice grains.

## The Worship for the Removal of Obstacles

The ritual for the removal of obstacles, the setting up of the ritual pavilion, and the worship of the **Divine Mothers** <note>Matrikas; a group of goddesses who protect the family and children</note> are performed together.
<gloss>6</gloss> Next follow the offering to the **All-Gods**, the **Stream of Wealth** <term>Vasordhara|A ritual where clarified butter (ghee) is poured in a continuous stream onto a wall or altar to symbolize a flow of prosperity</term>, and the **Ancestral Rite for Bliss** <term>Nandi-Shraddha|A joyful offering to ancestors performed specifically before happy occasions like weddings to seek their blessings</term>. || 1 ||

The worship for the removal of obstacles and the establishment of the **pavilion** <note>a temporary structure or altar space decorated for the ceremony</note> occur only during rituals such as **marriage**, the **sacred thread ceremony** <note>Upanayana; the initiation into Vedic study</note>, the **first haircut** <note>Chudakarana</note>, and the **parting of the hair** <note>Simantonnayana; a ritual performed for a pregnant woman's well-being</note>.

---

## Om. You are barley; drive away our haters, drive away our enemies. <note>original: "yavo'si yavayāsmadveṣo yavayārātīḥ"; this is a wordplay in Sanskrit where "Yava" (barley) sounds like the verb "Yavaya" (to drive away/separate)</note>
With this mantra, one should scatter barley grains. One should also scatter <term>Darbha|A sacred grass used in Vedic rituals for purification</term> and <term>Siddharthaka|White mustard seeds, believed to ward off evil spirits</term> silently, without reciting a mantra.

## Om. Growing from joint to joint, from knot to knot—O <term>Durva|Scutch grass (Cynodon dactylon), symbolizing longevity and spreading prosperity</term>, extend our life with a thousand and a hundred branches.
## With this mantra, one should throw sprouts of Durva grass into the pit.

## Om. I have praised Dadhikravan, the victorious, swift horse... <note>original: "dadhikrāvaṇo akāriṣam..."; an ancient Vedic verse dedicated to a divine horse, used here for purification and auspiciousness</note>

---

Again, the <term>Yajamana|The patron or householder who commissions the ritual</term> should dig the pit thoroughly while reciting the mantra "Om, may your digger not suffer harm..." <note>referring back to the mantra on page 102</note>. Then, saying the mantra "Om, they sprinkle, they sprinkle around...", he should sprinkle water into that pit.

Then, with the mantra "Om, you are barley...", he should place barley in that pit. And without a mantra, he should place <term>Kusha|Another name for the sacred Darbha grass</term> within it. Afterward, with the mantra "Om, from joint to joint...", he should place Durva grass in the pit.

# Om. May the mind, swift as thought, delight in the clarified butter; may Brihaspati extend this sacrifice; may he restore this sacrifice uninjured. May all the universal gods rejoice here. Om! Be established!
<note>original: "oṃ mano jūtijuṣatāmājyasya bṛhaspatiryajñamimaṃ tanotvariṣṭaṃ yyajñaṭhaṃ samimaṃ dadhātu | viśvedevāṃsa iha mādayantāmo3mpratiṣṭha" — This Vedic mantra (Yajurveda 2.13) is used here for the "Pratishtha" or the formal establishment and breathing of life into the ritual space.</note>

"May the deities of the pavilion be well-established and become granters of boons," having said this and established them. Then, after reciting "Om, salutations to the deities of the pavilion," one should worship them with either <term>Shodashopachara|The traditional sixteen-step hospitality ritual including bathing, dressing, and offering food to a deity</term> or <term>Panchopachara|A simplified five-step worship ritual</term>. 

Taking water in the hand, say: "For the pleasure of the pavilion deities, I shall feed the <term>Brahmanas|The priestly class of scholars and ritual specialists</term> according to my ability." After saying this, pour the water onto the ground. 

This establishment of the pavilion is performed during rites such as the <term>Simantonnayana|A traditional 'baby shower' or pregnancy ritual where the husband parts the wife's hair</term> and the <term>Annaprashana|The ritual ceremony of a child's first intake of solid food</term>...
<margin>Graha.
Pa.</margin>

---

Place a betel nut in five different spots upon a heap of <term>Akshata|Unbroken grains of rice symbolizing wholeness</term>. Recite the sequence from "Om, salutations to Nalini" to "I invoke Pashuvardhini." Then, taking rice in your hand, recite the mantra "Om. May the mind, swift as thought..." up to "May they be granters of boons," and then release the rice.
<note>This refers back to the list of five goddesses introduced on page 106. The betel nuts serve as physical representations (aniconic forms) of these goddesses during the ritual.</note>

After that, say "Om, salutations to the deities of the pavilion," and perform the worship of the five goddesses—Nalini and the others—using either the sixteen-fold or five-fold offerings of worship.

# [The establishment of the pavilion] is to be performed during the ceremonies of <term>Annaprashana|The ritual of a child's first intake of solid food</term>, <term>Chudakarana|The ritual of the first haircut or tonsure</term>, <term>Upanayana|The sacred thread initiation ceremony</term>, <term>Vedaramha|The formal beginning of Vedic studies</term>, <term>Keshanta|The first shaving of the beard</term>, <term>Vratavisarga|The conclusion of religious student vows</term>, and <term>Vivaha|Marriage</term>. In these matters, 
# traditional custom <note>original: "shishtachara" — the conduct of learned or respectable people in a community</note> is the only authority. Now, regarding the placement of the pillar for the purpose of the pavilion: When the sun is in the three <term>Rashis|Zodiac signs</term> of Taurus, Gemini, or Cancer, it should be done in the South-East. When the sun is in the three signs of Leo, Virgo, or Libra, it should be done in the North-East. 
# When the sun is in the three signs of Scorpio, Sagittarius, or Capricorn, it should be done in the North-West. When the sun is in the three signs of Aquarius, Pisces, or Aries, 
# it should be done in the South-West. Thus ends the establishment of the pavilion and the consecration of its deities.

---

Once again, the patron, taking water in his hand and reciting <term>"For the pleasure of the pavilion deities..."</term> <note>original: "maṇḍapadevatāprītyarthaṃ"</note>, should make a solemn vow to feed the <term>Brahmanas|Priests and scholars</term> and then pour the water onto the ground. This establishment of the pavilion is performed during the auspicious rites of <term>Simanta|A pregnancy ritual to ensure the health of the mother and child</term>, <term>Annaprashana</term>, <term>Mundan|Tonsure</term>, <term>Yajnopavita|Sacred thread ceremony</term>, <term>Vedaramha</term>, marriage, and other such events. In these matters, one should act according to the local customs of the region.

When the sun is situated in Taurus, Gemini, or Cancer, the pavilion pillar <term>(Mandwa)</term> should be placed in the <term>Agni-kon|The South-East direction, associated with the fire god Agni</term>. When the sun is in Leo, Virgo, or Libra, the said pillar should be in the <term>Ishan-kon|The North-East direction, associated with Shiva/Ishana</term>. When the sun is in Scorpio, Sagittarius, or Capricorn, it should be in the <term>Vayu-kon|The North-West direction, associated with the wind god Vayu</term>. And when the sun is situated in Aquarius, Pisces, or Aries, the pavilion pillar should be established in the <term>Nairitya-kon|The South-West direction, associated with the goddess Nirriti</term>.

->In this manner, the establishment of the pavilion and the consecration of the deities within the pavilion are concluded.<-

# Worship of the Sixteen Mothers
<note>original: "Shodasha-Matrika-Pujanam"</note>

<margin>Graha. Pa. 106 10</margin>
In the South-Eastern direction, one should perform the establishment of the <term>Mothers|The Shodasha Matrikas, a group of sixteen goddesses who protect and nourish</term> upon a wooden platform. This can be done using either small statues or heaps of <term>Akshata|Unbroken consecrated rice</term>, arranged in a sequence from East to West or from South to North. The procedure is as follows:

<margin>Ma. Pu. 106</margin>
> Near the group of Mothers, I establish Lord <term>Ganesha|The elephant-headed deity who removes obstacles</term>, 
> who is the remover of all obstacles and is worshipped across the three worlds.
> <note>original: "Samīpe mātṛvargasya..."</note>

> Om. O <term>Ganapati|Leader of the divine hosts</term>, we invoke you, the Lord of the hosts; we invoke you, the Lord of our loved ones; we invoke you, the Lord of our treasures...
> <note>original: "Gaṇānāṃ tvā gaṇapatiṃ havāmahe..." — a famous Vedic hymn to Ganesha used to invite his presence at the start of any ritual.</note>

---

**Worship of the Sixteen Mothers** — For auspicious ceremonies such as <term>Vivaha|Weddings</term>, one should worship the Sixteen Mothers in front of the Ganesha idol. This is done by forming sixteen small mounds out of <term>Gomaya-pinda|Purified cow dung</term> to represent the goddesses. Alternatively, one may place sixteen <term>Sopari|Betel nuts</term> on sixteen small heaps of consecrated rice on a wooden stool. The establishment of these Sixteen Mothers should proceed starting from either the East or the North, as follows:

<note>The list of names usually follows this section, starting with Gauri, Padma, Sachi, etc.</note>

**Technical Terms used in this ritual:**
- **Sixteen Mothers:** A group of protector goddesses invoked for blessings and the removal of spiritual hurdles.
- **Worship:** The act of offering devotion through specific rituals and prayers.
- **Ganapati:** Another name for Ganesha, the lord of beginnings.
- **Establishment:** The ritual process of "inviting" a deity into a physical object like a statue or a betel nut.
- **Cow-dung mound:** A traditional purifying substance used in Vedic rituals to create temporary altars.
- **Unbroken Rice:** Symbolizes wholeness and fertility in Hindu rites.
- **Betel Nut:** Often used as a substitute for a deity's physical form during worship.

# May the Mothers, beginning with Gauri and ending with the Family Deity, together with Ganapati, be well-established and grantors of boons.

->Gauri, Padma, Shachi, Medha, Savitri, Vijaya, Jaya,<-
<note>These are names of various forms of the Divine Mother, representing qualities like brilliance (Gauri), prosperity (Padma), and victory (Vijaya).</note>
->Devasena, Svadha, Svaha, the Mothers, the Mothers of the World. || 1 ||<-
<note>original: "gaurī padmā śacī medhā sāvitrī vijayā jayā | devasenā svadhā svāhā mātaro lokamātaraḥ ||1||"</note>
->Dhriti, Pushti, as well as Tushti, and one's own Family Deity.<-
<note>original: "dhṛtiḥ puṣṭistathā tuṣṭiḥ ātmanaḥ kuladevatāḥ |" — These names represent Patience (Dhriti), Nourishment (Pushti), and Contentment (Tushti).</note>
->With Ganesha as the additional seventeenth, these sixteen are to be worshipped during auspicious rites. || 2 ||<-
<note>original: "gaṇeśenādhikā hyetā vṛddhau pūjyāstu ṣoḍaśa ||2||" — While called the "Sixteen Mothers," Lord Ganesha is traditionally included as their protector, making seventeen figures in total.</note>

---

The <term>Yajamana</term> <note>the patron or person for whom the ritual is performed</note>, taking <term>Akshata</term> <note>consecrated, unbroken rice grains symbolizing wholeness</note> in hand, should recite the mantra starting from "Om. May the mind, the speed..." <note>referring to the Vedic mantra on page 124</note> up to the words "Be well-established and grantors of boons," and then sprinkle the rice upon the Sixteen Mothers. Furthermore, they should recite the two verses beginning with "Gauri, Padma, Shachi..." and ending with "these sixteen are to be worshipped during auspicious rites."

<note>This ritual action, called 'Akshata-prakshepa,' serves to focus the practitioner's intention and formally invite the divine presence into the ritual space.</note>

# The Worship of Vasodhara <note>literally "The Stream of Wealth," a ritual where clarified butter is poured in lines on a wall to invoke prosperity</note>

On the southeastern wall <note>the direction associated with Agni, the god of fire</note>, after decorating it with dots of saffron or similar pigments, and while reciting the following mantra, one should create seven streams with ghee <note>clarified butter</note>, moving either from west to east or from south to north.

> Om. You are the purifier of wealth, a hundred-fold; you are the purifier of wealth, a thousand-fold. May the divine Savitri <note>the solar deity</note> purify you with the hundred-fold purifier of wealth for well-being.
<note>original Sanskrit: "oṃ vasoḥ pavitramasi śatadhāraṃ vasoḥ pavitramasi sahasradhāram | devastvāṃ savitā punātu vasoḥ pavitreṇa śatadhāreṇa supvā ||"</note>

The streams of wealth <term>Vasodhara</term> must be performed with this mantra. With the mantra "Om. May it yield my desires..." one should then blend the streams with jaggery <note>unrefined cane sugar</note> for half of their length. One should invoke a specific deity for each individual stream.

---

<note>Worship of Vasodhara (The Seven Mothers of Ghee)—On the wall or a ritual wooden stool, in the southeastern corner, write the word **Shree** <note>representing the Goddess of Fortune</note> using red lead or vermilion. Below it, decorate by making seven dots in sequence: one at the top, two below that, three below that, and so on until seven dots are formed.</note>

<summary>This page provides instructions for the Vasodhara ritual, involving the creation of seven symbolic streams of ghee on a wall to ensure prosperity. It details the specific Vedic mantra for the offering and the method of decorating the ritual space with vermilion and jaggery.</summary>

# Recitation of the Longevity Mantra (The Text). Then the Brahmins recite:

->**"That long life which the gods bestowed upon those who live until the end of seven world-cycles—**<-
->**endowed with that same life, may we live for a hundred autumns."**<note>original: "śaradaḥ śatam"; a classic Vedic expression for a full, ideal human lifespan of 100 years. The "seven world-cycles" (kalpas) refer to the immense spans of time lived by the immortals or chiranjivis.</note> **(1)**<-

->**"Long-lived are the serpents, the mountains, and the rivers; infinite are the seven oceans and the cardinal directions.**<-
->**By that same infinite life, may we live for a hundred autumns." (2)**<-

->**"The five elements are eternal and free from destruction.**<-
->**Likewise, with an indestructible life, may we live for a hundred autumns."**<note>original: "pañca-bhūtāni"; these are the five great elements—Earth, Water, Fire, Air, and Ether—which are considered the permanent building blocks of the universe.</note> **(3)**<-

# Procedure for the Ancestral Rite of Joy (Nandishraddha)

Thereafter, one should perform the Nandishraddha <term>Nandishraddha: A celebratory ancestral rite performed before auspicious events like weddings or births, unlike the somber funeral rites</term> according to the symbolic method <term>Sankalpika-vidhi: A simplified ritual procedure where the primary focus is the formal declaration of intent (Sankalpa) rather than elaborate physical offerings</term>. It is as follows:
Having spread straight Kusha grass <note>original: "ऋजून् कुशानास्तीर्य"; sacred grass used in Hindu rituals to purify the space and provide seats for deities or spirits</note> in four places in a clockwise direction in the middle of the leaf-plates, one should perform the worship preceded by a formal declaration of intent. This particular ancestral rite should be performed only in the "Savya" position <note>original: "सव्येन एव"; the sacred thread is worn over the left shoulder, which is the standard position for joyful ceremonies, as opposed to the right-shoulder position used for funeral rites</note>.

<margin>
Procedure for Joy (Nandi-prayoga)
Page 136
</margin>

Om. To the Universal Gods <term>Visvedevas: A group of deities who represent the collective powers of the universe</term> named Satyavasu, who are the "Faces of Joy" <note>original: "नान्दीमुखाः" (Nandimukha); a title given to ancestors and deities when they are invoked for happy occasions</note>: Om Earth, Atmosphere, Heavens. This is the water for your feet, the washing of your feet, the cleansing of your feet; may there be prosperity. 

Om. To the Mother, the Paternal Grandmother, and the Paternal Great-Grandmother, who are the "Faces of Joy": Om Earth, Atmosphere, Heavens. This is the water for your feet, the washing of your feet, the cleansing of your feet; may there be prosperity.

---

**Procedure for the Ancestral Rite of Joy** — Following that, one should perform the Nandishraddha solely through the formal declaration of intent (Sankalpa). The method is as follows: Toward the East, on the seat designated for the Universal Gods, one should place Kusha grass with the tips pointing North. Then, place three seats starting from the South, arranged with the tips of the grass pointing East: the first seat is for the Mother, Paternal Grandmother, and Paternal Great-Grandmother; the second seat is for the Father, Paternal Grandfather, and Paternal Great-Grandfather; and the third is for those accompanied by their wives... <note>The text here describes the physical layout of the ritual space, ensuring each generation of ancestors is properly seated and oriented according to sacred geometry.</note>

---

1. In the *Bhavishya Purana* <note>One of the eighteen major ancient encyclopedic texts of Hinduism</note>: "O King! One may or may not perform the offering of rice-balls <term>Pinda-nirvapana: The act of offering cooked rice balls to the deceased</term>. In the Shraddha performed for prosperity <term>Vriddhi-shraddha: Another name for the Nandishraddha, performed to increase the family's well-being</term>, O mighty-armed one, one must look to the specific traditions of one's own family."
2. Without the words "the deceased," without mentioning specific forms or lineages <term>Gotra: The paternal lineage or clan name</term>, without names, with food, and without the use of sesame seeds <note>Sesame seeds are typically used in funeral rites but are often excluded from these joyful ancestral rites to maintain a celebratory atmosphere</note>, the Nandishraddha is performed with the sacred thread over the left shoulder.

### Offering the Seat

Om. O Universal Gods named Satyavasu, who are the "Faces of Joy": Om Earth, Atmosphere, Heaven. These [two] are the seats... <note>original: "इमे आसने" refers to the ritual seats offered to the deities</note>

One should prepare a third seat for the maternal grandfather, maternal great-grandfather, and maternal great-great-grandfather. This seat should not be touching the others. On those four seats, one should worship the ancestors along with the Universal Gods <term>Visvedevas: The collective deities who witness and protect the ritual</term> in sequence. The order is as follows: on a leaf-plate, place four straight blades of Kusha grass <note>sacred grass used in Hindu rituals to purify the space</note> in order from East to South, and perform the worship with a formal declaration of intent <term>Sankalpa: A ritual statement of purpose and identity</term>. Recite the sentence from "Om, O Mothers, Grandmothers, and Great-Grandmothers..." up to "...cleansing the feet, prosperity."

# The Offering of Water with Milk and Barley
<note>original: "Sa-kshira-yavamudakadanam"</note>

May the Universal Gods <term>Vishvedevas</term> known as Satyavasu, who are the "Faces of Joy" <term>Nandimukhas: ancestors and deities invoked during auspicious occasions</term>, be pleased. May the maternal lineage—the mother, grandmother, and great-grandmother—the "Faces of Joy," be pleased. May the paternal lineage—the father, grandfather, and great-grandfather—the "Faces of Joy," be pleased. May the maternal grandfathers, maternal great-grandfathers, and maternal great-great-grandfathers along with their wives, the "Faces of Joy," be pleased. In these four locations—"May the waters be auspicious," thus [one offers] the water. "May there be goodwill," thus [one offers] the flower. "May there be unbroken grains and may there be no harm," thus [one offers] the unbroken grains <term>akshata: whole rice grains used in rituals to symbolize permanence</term>. Om.

---

**The Offering of Water with Milk and Barley** — Placing a mixture of milk, barley, and water in an earthenware vessel <term>mrittika patra</term>, take it in the right hand and recite from "The Universal Gods known as Satyavasu" <note>original: "Satyavasu-sangyakah"</note> up to "be pleased" <note>original: "priyantam"</note>, then pour the water upon the seat representing the Universal Gods. 

Again, reciting from "the mother, grandmother, and great-grandmother" up to "be pleased," pour the water-milk mixture upon the seat of the mother, grandmother, and great-grandmother. Then, reading the sentence from "the father, grandfather, and great-grandfather" up to "be pleased," pour the said water upon the seat of the father, grandfather, and great-grandfather. 

In the same manner, reciting from "the maternal grandfather, great-grandfather, and great-great-grandfather" up to "be pleased," pour the water from that earthen bowl <term>kasora: a small lid-like clay bowl</term> upon the seat of the maternal grandfather, great-grandfather, and great-great-grandfather along with their wives.

**Vocabulary:**
**Offering of water with milk and barley** <note>original: "sa-kshira-yavamudakadanam"</note>; **Faces of Joy** <note>original: "nandimukha"</note>; **Universal Gods** <note>original: "vishvedevah"</note>; **Along with their wives** <note>original: "sapatnikah"</note>; **Paternal ancestors (three generations)** <note>original: "pitru-pitamaha-prapitamahah"</note>; **Earthenware vessel** <note>original: "mrittika patra"</note>; **Small clay bowl** <note>original: "kasore"</note>.

# Giving of the Ritual Fee

-> Om. To the Universal Gods <term>Vishvedevas</term> known as Satya and Vasu, who are the "Faces of Joy" <term>Nandimukha</term>; Om, in the earth, atmosphere, and heavens; for the sake of attaining the fruit, the consecration, and the perfection of the performed Ancestral Rite of Joy <term>Nandishraddha</term>, I release this ritual fee <term>Dakshina</term> consisting of the value of grapes, Indian gooseberry, barley, and ginger root. <-

-> Om. To the Mothers, paternal Grandmothers, and paternal Great-Grandmothers, who are the "Faces of Joy"; Om, in the earth, atmosphere, and heavens; for the sake of attaining the fruit, the consecration, and the perfection of the performed Ancestral Rite of Joy, I release this ritual fee consisting of the value of grapes, Indian gooseberry, barley, and ginger root. <-

-> Om. To the Fathers, paternal Grandfathers, and paternal Great-Grandfathers... <-

---

Again, the patron <term>yajamana</term>, with hands folded in prayer, should address the priests <term>Brahmins</term> by reciting the prayers from "Om, may our lineage increase" to "May these blessings be true." The assembly of priests should also respond, "May these blessings be true."

**Giving of the Ritual Fee:** Having recited from "Om, to the Universal Gods known as Satya and Vasu..." <note>original: "Om satyavasusamjnakah vishvedevah"</note> until "...I release this ritual fee" <note>original: "dakshinam datumahmutsrije"</note>, the patron should offer the ritual fee—consisting of the value of raisins, Indian gooseberry, barley, and ginger root etc.—upon the seat of the Universal Gods. Then, from "Om, to the Mothers, paternal Grandmothers, and paternal Great-Grandmothers..."

---

> 1. The Mother, the paternal Grandmother, and likewise the paternal Great-Grandmother; the Father, the paternal Grandfather, and likewise the paternal Great-Grandfather. || 1 ||
> 2. The maternal Grandfather, his father, the maternal Great-Grandfather, and so on. May all these ancestors be well-pleased and bestow auspiciousness. || 2 ||

<gloss>
**Nandishraddha**: A "joyful" ancestral rite performed before auspicious occasions like weddings or planet pacification.
**Grahashanti**: A ritual performed to appease or balance the influences of the nine celestial planets.
**Acharyadivarana**: The formal selection and ritual "hiring" of the head priest and his assistants.
**Yajamana**: The patron or host who commissions the ritual and receives its spiritual benefits.
**Vajasaney-Madhyandina Shakha**: A specific tradition or "branch" of the White Yajur Veda, common in North India.
**Varandravya**: The physical gifts (clothes, money, etc.) used to formally request a priest's service.
</gloss>

<margin>Ritual for Planets, Page 162</margin>
**Sequence for installing deities on the Sarvatobhadra and Lingatobhadra** — On a square wooden platform, one or two cubits <note>A 'cubit' (hasta) is approximately 18 inches, the length from the elbow to the tip of the middle finger.</note> in length and width, construct the <term>Sarvatobhadra</term> <note>literally "Auspicious on all sides"; a complex 81- or 324-square grid used as a celestial map for deities.</note> and <term>Lingatobhadra</term> <note>A variation of the sacred grid specifically dedicated to forms of Shiva.</note> diagrams using thread and red powder. After installing and worshipping the respective deities upon it, place a copper or clay <term>Kalasha</term> <note>A ritual water pot representing the universe or the womb of creation.</note> in the center of that platform according to the rules. Upon that pot, after performing the <term>Agnyuttarana</term> <note>original: "अग्न्युत्तारण"; a ritual "lifting" or purification by fire to prepare an image for worship.</note> and the <term>Prana-Pratishtha</term> <note>The "consecration of breath," a ritual that invites the divine essence into a physical statue.</note>, one should install and worship the primary golden idol. The method is as follows:

१. **Verses on the Sarvatobhadra from the Skanda Purana:** Draw nineteen lines running from the East and from the North <note>This creates an 18x18 grid of 324 small squares.</note>. There is a white three-step "half-moon" <note>original: "khandendu"; a crescent shape in the design.</note>, and five black "chains." ॥ १ ॥
->There is an eleven-cell blue "vine," and a red "auspicious square" <note>original: "bhadram"</note> of nine cells. There is a white "pond" <note>original: "vapi"</note> of twenty-four cells and a yellow "perimeter" of twenty cells. ॥ २ ॥<-
->In the center, with sixteen cells, is a red lotus with its seed-head. The lotus is surrounded by the perimeter, and outside of that are the three qualities of nature: Purity, Passion, and Inertia <note>original: "sattva, rajas, tamas"; the three fundamental strands or "gunas" that make up the material world.</note>.<-
<margin>Sarvatobhadra Installation, 162</margin>
->In the center of this, one should install the deities, starting with Brahma and the Lords of the Gods. ॥ ३ ॥<-

२. **Verses on the Lingatobhadra from the Skanda Purana:** Eighteen lines are prescribed for the creation of the **Four-Linga** pattern <note>This creates a 17x17 grid.</note>. At the corners are white three-step "moons," and with three steps are the black "chains." ॥ १ ॥
->The blue "vine" consists of seven cells, and the red "auspicious square" is four cells. Beside the square is the Great Rudra <note>A fierce form of Shiva.</note>, colored black and occupying eighteen cells. ॥ २ ॥<-

# Sequence for Installing the Deities of the Vedic Sarvatobhadra and Lingatobhadra Mandalas. It is as follows:

> Om. Brahma was born first in the ancient days; from the radiant horizon, the Seer revealed him. He reveals the highest forms of this world, the womb of the existent and the non-existent. <note>original: "ॐ ब्रह्म॑ जज्ञा॒नं..." This is a famous Vedic hymn (the Brahma-Jajñānam mantra) used to invoke the creative power of the universe. It describes the birth of the Great Creator from the primordial light.</note>

-> (In the center of the lotus-heart) Om. Earth, Atmosphere, Heavens. Salutations to Brahma. I invoke and install Lord Brahma. || 1 || <-

---

One should create a white-colored "well" <note>A 'vapi' or well refers to a specific rectangular section within the geometric grid of the mandala.</note> of five squares beside the position of Shiva. Similarly, one square should be colored yellow in the middle of the auspicious wells. || 3 ||

At the head of the "chain" <note>A 'shringkhala' is a decorative border or interlocking pattern in the diagram.</note>, one should make three squares yellow. From the "shoulders" of the <term>Lingas</term> <note>Abstract symbols representing the infinite nature of Shiva.</note>, twenty compartments should be colored red. || 4 ||

The perimeter is traditionally known to consist of sixteen yellow-colored squares. Afterwards, with nine squares, there should be a red square containing a <term>karnika</term> <note>The central seed-vessel or pericarp of a lotus design.</note>. || 5 ||

<margin>The five colors are described in the **Pancharatra** <note>An ancient collection of texts detailing temple construction and ritual arts.</note>:</margin> One should prepare five colored powders for the purpose of the <term>Mandala</term> <note>A sacred geometric diagram representing the cosmos.</note>. White is produced from powdered rice or from barley. || 1 ||

Red is obtained from safflower, vermilion, or from red ochre. Yellow is produced from yellow orpiment or sometimes from turmeric. || 2 ||

Black is to be made from burnt barley, and green from powdered <term>Bilva</term> <note>The wood-apple tree, sacred to Shiva; its dried leaves produce a vibrant green powder.</note> leaves. Or, one may construct the diagram using various colored grains to make it beautiful. || 3 ||

*Om. # The Rite of Fire-Purification
<note>original: "अग्न्युत्तारणविधिः" (Agnyuttarana-vidhi). This ritual, literally meaning "lifting out of the fire," is a symbolic cooling and purification rite. After an icon is crafted and spiritually "heated" by the artisan's tools or previous rites, it is bathed in cooling substances like ghee and water to prepare it for the infusion of life.</note>

In that ceremony, the presiding teacher (<term>Acharya</term>) should place the icon in a separate vessel, anoint it with <term>ghee</term> <note>clarified butter, used in rituals for its purifying and nourishing qualities</note>, and pour a continuous stream of water over it. The sacred chants (<term>mantras</term>) for this are:

> Om. O Fire, we surround you with the water-plants of the ocean. Be a purifier and bring us peace. || 1 ||
> <note>original: "ॐ समुद्रस्य त्वावक्याग्ने परिंव्ययामसि । पावुकोऽस्मन्भ्यं शिवो भव ॥"</note>
>
> Om. O Fire, we surround you with the covering of snow. Be a purifier and bring us peace. || 2 ||
> <note>original: "ॐ हिमस्य त्वा जरायुणाग्ने परिंव्ययामसि । पावुको अस्मन्भ्यं शिवो भव ॥"</note>
>
> Om. Descend upon the reeds, descend into the rivers. O Fire, you are the very essence of the waters...
> <note>original: "ॐ उप जमनुप वेतसेऽवतर नदीष्वा । अग्ने पित्तमपामसि"</note>

---

**The Procedure for Fire-Purification:** The teacher should take the golden icon of the deity that is to be installed and consecrated (<term>Prana-pratishtha</term>) and place it inside a silver vessel. He should then apply ghee to the icon. While reciting twelve specific mantras—beginning with "Om, of the ocean, you..." and ending with "...be auspicious for us"—he should pour a steady stream of water over the icon.

->Thus ends the Rite of Fire-Purification.<-

<note>While only three mantras are written in full in the Sanskrit section above, the ritual instructions specify a total of twelve verses to be recited during the water-pouring phase.</note>

<summary>This page details the Agnyuttarana-vidhi, a purification ritual where a golden deity icon is anointed with ghee and bathed in water while reciting Vedic mantras. This cooling rite is a prerequisite for the final consecration of the icon.</summary>

<keywords>Agnyuttarana, Fire-Purification, Ghee, Golden Icon, Prana-pratishtha, Silver Vessel, Vedic Mantras, Ritual Bathing</keywords>

Om. O water-spirit, come with those cooling rains; make this sacrifice of ours auspicious, O you of purifying color. || 3 ||
<note>original: "मण्डूकि ताभिरागहि..." (Manduki tabhiragahi...). While the literal word 'Manduki' means a female frog, in this Vedic context, it refers to the spirit of the rain and water-plants used to cool the ritual heat. The "purifying color" refers to the bright, clean nature of water and fire.</note>

Om. This is the gathering place of the waters, the very home of the ocean. May your scorching flames burn elsewhere, away from us; as a Purifier, be auspicious to us. || 4 ||

*Hrīm krom yam ram lam vam śam ṣam sam ham saḥ.* In this **image**, may the **life-breaths** <note>original: "prāṇāḥ"; refers to the vital internal energies</note> be present; here are the life-breaths. (Repeat)

## May the life-breaths be established in this image; may her life-breaths flow.
## May this image possess divinity for the sake of worship; may she be highly honored by all. <note>original: "asyai devatvamarcāyai māmaheti ca kaścana"</note>

---

The presiding priest of the **Consecration of the Life-Breath** <note>original: "Prāṇapratiṣṭhā-ācārya"</note> should hold the primary image in his left hand and cover it with his right hand. While doing so, he should recite the **seed-syllables** <note>original: "bīja-mantra"; potent, monosyllabic sounds that act as "seeds" for spiritual power</note> starting from "Om Ām Hrīm Krom" up until "remain happily for a long time, *Svāhā!*" as well as the **verse** <note>original: "śloka"</note> beginning with "May the life-breaths be established..." After performing the consecration, he should place the image on top of the **sacred water-jar** <note>original: "kalaśa"; a consecrated pot representing the universe or the deity’s body</note>.

<summary>This page details the specific mantras and physical gestures used to transition a ritual object from an inert statue to a living vessel for the deity, concluding with the image being placed on a sacred water-jar.</summary>

# Installation and Worship of the Sun and Other Planets

# Then, having spread a white cloth over the previously prepared square planetary altar (measuring one <term>Hasta</term> <note>a traditional unit of measurement roughly equal to the length of a forearm, about 18 inches</note>), draw the <term>Navagraha Mandala</term> <note>a sacred geometric grid or diagram representing the nine celestial bodies</note>. Perform the installation and worship of the Sun and other planets in the central and surrounding squares, according to their specified directions and sub-directions. The procedure is as follows:

->Installation and Worship of the Sun and other Nine Planets—On a square stool, spread a white cloth and use <term>Rori</term> <note>a sacred red powder made of turmeric and lime</note> and a thread to create the Nine-Planet Diagram. In the central square and the various directions and sub-directions, perform the invocation, installation, and worship of the Sun and other planets. It is done in this manner:<-

---

## 1. The Sequence of Installing the Planets according to the *Skanda Purana*:
<note>The Skanda Purana is one of the eighteen major Hindu religious texts, containing detailed instructions for various rituals.</note>

> After creating the mandala in the Northeast, one should proceed with the installation of the planets. The Sun is represented as a circle, and the Moon as a half-moon (crescent).
<note>original Sanskrit: "vṛttamaṇḍalamādityamardhacandraṃ niśākaram"</note>

> Mars is represented as a triangle, and Mercury in the shape of a bow. Jupiter is said to be an eight-petaled lotus, and Venus is a four-sided square.

> Know Saturn to be in a human form, and Rahu in the shape of a crocodile. Ketu should be recognized as a sword-shape within the auspicious planetary mandala.

## An Alternative Method:

> The Sun is a circle, and the Moon is a square. Mars is a triangle, and Mercury is like an arrow.

> For Jupiter, the shape is that of a <term>Pattisha</term> <note>a type of ancient spear or halberd with a sharp edge</note>, and for Venus, a pentagon. For Saturn, a bow-shape, and for Rahu, the shape of a <term>Surpa</term> <note>a traditional flat winnowing basket used for grain</note>.

It cites the Skanda Purana to define the distinct shapes—such as circles, triangles, and lotuses—associated with each planet.</summary>
