# I invoke the Sun, who resembles the hibiscus flower in glow, the son of Kashyapa, possessed of great radiance, the enemy of darkness, and the destroyer of all sins.
<note>This is a "Dhyana Shloka," a verse used to visualize the deity. Original Sanskrit: "japākusumasaṅkāśaṃ kāśyapeyaṃ mahādyutim | tamo'riṃ sarvapāpaghnaṃ sūryamāvāhayāmyaham ||"</note>

# Om. Moving through the dark firmament, sustaining the immortal and the mortal, the divine Savitar <note>an aspect of the Sun-god associated with the light of sunrise and stimulation of life</note> comes on his golden chariot, beholding all the worlds.
<note>This is a famous Vedic mantra from the Rig Veda (1.35.2) used during the installation of the Sun. Original Sanskrit: "oṃ ā kṛṣṇena rajasā varttamāno niveśayannamṛtaṃ martyañca | hiraṇyayena savitā rathenā devo yāti bhuvanāni paśyan ||"</note>

---

For Ketu, the shape of a flag should be drawn, following the sequence of the <term>Mandalas</term> <note>sacred geometric diagrams</note>. It should be known that Venus and the Sun face East; Jupiter and Mercury face North. 

Saturn and the Moon face West, while the remaining planets <note>Mars, Rahu, and Ketu</note> face South. In the center, one should place the Sun; in the Southeast, the Moon. 

In the South, one should place Mars; in the Northeast, Mercury. In the North, one should place Jupiter; and in the East, Venus. 

In the West, one should place Saturn; in the Southwest, Rahu. In the Northwest, Ketu. Such is the proper arrangement of the planets. 

All of them face toward the Sun, accompanied by their <term>Adhidevatas</term> <note>primary presiding deities</note> and <term>Pratyadhidevatas</term> <note>secondary presiding deities</note>. The primary deity is placed to the right, and the secondary deity to the left. 

The Sun and Mars are reddish-red; Venus and the Moon are white. Mercury is green-colored, and Jupiter is yellow. 

->Saturn, Rahu, and Ketu are likewise black-colored.<-

**Om. Earth, Atmosphere, Heavens! O Sun, born in the land of Kalinga, belonging to the lineage of Sage Kashyapa, of red complexion! O Sun!**
**Come here, stay here; salutations to the Sun. I invoke the Sun and establish him here. || 1 ||**
<note>This is the "Prana Pratishtha" or life-infusing formula. It identifies the Sun's mythological "gotra" (lineage) and his traditional place of origin (Kalinga, modern-day Odisha).</note>

**I invoke the Moon (Soma), who resembles the color of curd, a conch shell, and snow; who was born from the Ocean of Milk, the Lord of moonlight and the Master of the night.**
<note>original: "dadhi-śaṅkha-tuṣārābhaṃ kṣīrodārṇavasambhavam | jyotsnāpatiṃ niśānāthaṃ somamāvāhayāmyaham ||" This verse describes the Moon's cooling, white nature, contrasting with the Sun's heat.</note>

**Om. O Gods, empower this man to be without rivals, for great lordship, for great supremacy, for great dominion over the people, and for the strength of Indra. This man, the son of <insert>Mother's Name</insert> and the son of <insert>Father's Name</insert>, is your King, O people. Soma is the King of us, the priests.**
<note>This is a famous Vedic mantra from the Shukla Yajurveda (9.40). Though originally a coronation hymn for a human king, in this context, it is used to invoke the royal power of Soma (the Moon), who is traditionally called the "King of the Brahmins."</note>

---

<note>Reciting the verse ‘Resembling the hibiscus flower...’ <note>See page 234 for the full verse</note> and the mantra ‘Om, moving through the dark firmament...’ up to the phrase ‘I invoke and establish the Sun,’ one should perform the invocation, installation, and worship of the Sun. || 1 ||</note>

**Vocabulary used in this ritual:**
*   **Sun (Surya):** The primary solar deity.
*   **Moon (Soma):** The lunar deity, also associated with the sacred ritual drink.
*   **Invocation (<term>Avahana</term>):** The act of calling a deity to be present in an image or diagram.
*   **Installation (<term>Sthapana</term>):** Fixing the deity's presence in the ritual space.
*   **Worship (<term>Pujana</term>):** The act of offering honors such as flowers, incense, or water.
*   **Born in Kalinga:** A traditional geographical association for the Sun.
*   **Kashyapa Lineage:** The mythological family to which the Sun belongs.
*   **Born from the Ocean of Milk:** A reference to the "Churning of the Ocean" myth where the Moon emerged.
*   **Master of the Night:** An epithet for the Moon.
*   **Supremacy (<term>Jyaishthyaya</term>):** Higher rank or seniority.

<note>Bhojakata is an ancient region often identified with parts of Vidarbha in central India. The Bhrigu lineage (Bhargava) refers to one of the most ancient and influential families of seers in Vedic tradition.</note>

### ### O Venus, come here, stay here; salutations to Venus. I invoke Venus and establish him here. || 6 ||

->**I invoke Saturn, who has the luster of a blue lotus, who is the son of the Sun and the elder brother of Yama, the Lord of Death.**<-
<note>original: "nīlāmbujasamābhāsaṃ raviputraṃ yamāgrajam |"</note>
->**I invoke him who was born to the Sun-god and his wife, Chhaya (Shadow).**<-
<note>original: "chāyāmārtaṇḍa-sambhūtaṃ śanimāvāhayāmyaham ||"</note>
<note>Saturn, or Shani, is depicted as a dark-complexioned deity. In mythology, his mother Chhaya was the shadow-form of the Sun's wife, Saranyu. His relationship as the brother of Yama reflects Saturn's role in delivering the results of one's past actions (karma).</note>

### ### Om. May the divine waters be for our aid and for our drinking. May they flow over us with peace and health.
<note>original: "oṃ śaṃ no devīrabhiṣṭaya āpo bhavantu pītaye | śaṃ yorabhisravantu naḥ ||"</note>
<note>This is a famous Vedic verse from the Rig Veda. Although it addresses the waters, it is traditionally used as the primary mantra for the planet Saturn because the first syllable "Sham" is phonetically linked to his name and his pacifying energy.</note>

### ### Om. Earth, Atmosphere, Heavens! O Saturn, born in the land of Saurashtra, belonging to the lineage of Sage Kashyapa, of black complexion! 
<note>Saurashtra refers to the coastal region of modern-day Gujarat. Sage Kashyapa is a foundational figure in Hindu genealogy, considered the father of many celestial beings.</note>

### ### O Saturn, come here, stay here; salutations to Saturn. I invoke Saturn and establish him here. || 7 ||

## I invoke Rahu, who has half a body and great valor, the subduer of the Moon and the Sun, born from the womb of Simhika.
<note>original: "ardhakāyaṃ mahāvīryaṃ candrādityavimardanam | siṃhikāgarbhasambhūtaṃ rāhumāvāhayāmyaham ||"</note>
<note>In Hindu mythology, Rahu is the severed head of a demon who causes eclipses by "swallowing" the Sun and Moon. His mother, Simhika, is a prominent figure in Puranic lore. He represents the North Node of the Moon.</note>

## Om. With what assistance shall he, the wonderful, ever-prospering friend, be present for us? With what most mighty aid?
<note>original: "oṃ kayā naścitra ābhuvadūtī sadāvṛdhaḥ sakhā | kayā śaciṣṭhayā vṛtā ||"</note>
<note>This is a Vedic verse from the Rig Veda (4.31.1). Although originally addressed to Indra, it is traditionally used in liturgy to invoke Rahu due to specific phonetic and symbolic associations in the priestly manuals.</note>

# Installation and Worship of the Overlord Deities

As follows:

->**I invoke that Lord (Ishvara), who has five faces, is mounted upon a bull, is the husband of Uma, has three eyes, and carries an excellent skull-topped staff.**<-
<note>original: "pañcavaktraṃ vṛṣārūḍhamumeśaṃ ca trilocanam | āvāhayāmīśvaraṃ taṃ khaṭvāṅgavaradhāriṇam ||"</note>

->**Om. We worship the Three-Eyed One, who is fragrant and nourishes prosperity. As a cucumber is freed from its bond to the vine, may he liberate us from death for the sake of immortality.**<-
<note>original: "oṃ tryambakaṃ yajāmahe sugandhiṃ puṣṭivarddhanam | urvārukamiva bandhanānmṛtyormukṣīya mā’mṛtāt ||"</note>
<note>This is the famous Maha Mrityunjaya Mantra (Great Death-Conquering Mantra) from the Rig Veda (7.59.12), used here to invoke the life-preserving aspect of Shiva.</note>

### Technical Vocabulary
*   **White-complexioned (<term>Shukla-varna</term>):** A color symbolizing purity and sattvic (harmonious) qualities.
*   **Large-eyed (<term>Vishalakshi</term>):** An epithet for beauty and all-seeing wisdom.
*   **Tortoise-back (<term>Kurma-prishta</term>):** Refers to the Earth resting on the cosmic tortoise.
*   **Earth (<term>Dhara</term> / <term>Prithvi</term>):** The personified goddess of the land and fertility.
*   **Invocation (<term>Avahana</term>):** The ritual act of calling a deity to be present in an image or altar.
*   **Pleasant Earth (<term>Syona Prithvi</term>):** A specific Vedic address to the ground we walk upon.
*   **Shelter/Peace (<term>Sharmma</term>):** Divine protection or a state of bliss.
*   **Lord Vishnu:** The supreme deity responsible for the protection and maintenance of the cosmic order (<term>Dharma</term>).
*   **Garuda-mount (<term>Garuda-vahana</term>):** The celestial eagle-man who serves as Vishnu's vehicle.
*   **Crown and Earrings (<term>Kirita-kundala</term>):** Standard royal regalia signifying divine sovereignty.

It emphasizes the Earth's role as a provider of food and safety and Vishnu's role as a royal protector.</summary>

<vocab>
<term>Vastoshpati</term>: The "Lord of the Dwelling," a deity presiding over the architecture and the physical foundation of a home.
<term>Invocation</term> (Avahana): The ritual act of inviting a deity to be present at the ceremony.
<term>Establishment</term> (Sthapana): The ritual act of "fixing" the divine presence into an object, such as a pot or an image.
<term>Worship</term> (Pujana): The act of offering items like water, flowers, and incense to the deity.
<term>Two-legged</term> (Dvipade): A poetic reference to humans.
<term>Four-legged</term> (Chatushpade): A poetic reference to cattle, horses, and pets.
<term>Intermediary Directions</term> (Vidik): Refers to the secondary compass points (NE, SE, SW, NW), indicating the deity's pervasive presence.
</vocab>

# Invocation and Worship of the Ten Directional Guardians and Others

Outside the <term>Mandala</term> <note>a sacred geometric diagram representing the cosmos</note>, one should invoke the <term>Dashadikpala</term> <note>the ten guardians of the cardinal and intermediate directions, as well as the zenith and nadir</note>.

> I invoke Indra, the best of the lords of the gods, who holds the <term>Vajra</term> <note>the thunderbolt weapon</note> in his hand and possesses great strength; I call upon the Lord of a hundred sacrifices for the successful completion of this ritual.
<note>original: "indraṃ surapatiśreṣṭhaṃ vajrahastaṃ mahābalam | āvāhaye yajñasiddhyai śatayajñādhipaṃ prabhum ||" In Hindu mythology, Indra's status as "Lord of a hundred sacrifices" (Shatakratu) refers to the merit required to attain his throne.</note>

> Om. Indra the protector, Indra the savior, Indra who is easily reached in every call, the hero Indra; I call upon the powerful one, Indra who is invoked by many; may the bountiful <term>Maghavan</term> <note>an epithet of Indra meaning "the generous benefactor"</note> bestow well-being upon us.
<note>original: "oṃ trātāramindramavitāramindraꣳ have have suhavaꣳ śūramindram | hvayāmi śakraṃ puruhūtamindraꣳ svasti no maghavā dhāttvindraḥ —" This is a Vedic hymn from the Rig Veda (6.47.11) and Shukla Yajurveda (20.50) used to ensure divine protection during the ceremony.</note>

> Om. Earth, Atmosphere, Heavens. O Indra, come here, stay here. Salutations to Indra; I invoke Indra and establish him here. || 1 ||
<note>original: "oṃ bhūrbhuvaḥ svaḥ indrehāgaccha iha tiṣṭha indrāya namaḥ, indramāvāhayāmi sthāpayāmi || 1 ||" This is the standard liturgical formula for "fixing" a deity's presence into an object or space during a rite.</note>

<note>1. According to the Compendium: Rudra, Agni, the Lord of the Ancestors (Yama), Nairrita, Varuna, Vayu, Kubera, Isha, Brahma, and Ananta are the ten Lords of the Directions.
original: "saṃgrahe—rudro vahniḥ pitṛpatirnairṛto varuṇo marut | kubera īśo brahmā ca hyananto daśa dikpatiḥ ||" This list corresponds to the directions: NE, SE, S, SW, W, NW, N, NE (alternate), Up, and Down.</note>

> I invoke Agni, the Fire God, who has three feet, seven hands, two heads, and two noses; who possesses six eyes and four ears.
<note>original: "tripādaṃ saptahastaṃ ca dvimūrddhānaṃ dvināsikam | ṣaṇnetraṃ ca catuḥśrotramagnimāvāhayāmyaham ||" This verse describes the esoteric form of Agni; his seven hands represent the seven tongues of flame, and his three legs symbolize the three worlds or types of sacred fire.</note>

> Om. O Agni, you are a God; protect our generous patrons with your divine guardians, O worshipful one. You are the protector of our children, our descendants, and our cattle, ever-watchful according to your sacred law.
<note>original: "oṃ tvaṃ no agne tava deva pāyubhirmmaghono rakṣa tvamāśva vandya | trātā tokasya tanaye gavāmasya nimeṣṛṣṭha rakṣamāṇastava vrate |" This is a Vedic prayer for protection and prosperity, ensuring the safety of the household and lineage through the power of the sacrificial fire.</note>

> Om. Earth, Atmosphere, Heavens. O Agni, come here, stay here. Salutations to Agni; I invoke Agni and establish him here. || 2 ||
<note>original: "oṃ bhūrbhuvaḥ svaḥ agne ihāgaccha iha tiṣṭha agnaye namaḥ, agnimāvāhayāmi sthāpayāmi || 2 ||" This formula concludes the invocation, inviting the deity into the specific physical space of the ritual.</note>

## I invoke Yama for the protection of this sacrifice—he who is of immense strength, mounted upon a great buffalo, and holding a staff in his hand.
<note>original: "mahāmahiṣamārūḍhaṃ daṇḍahastaṃ mahābalam | yajñasaṃrakṣaṇārthāya yamamāvāhayāmyaham ||" This verse describes Yama's traditional iconography. His mount, the buffalo, represents endurance and strength, while his staff (danda) symbolizes his role as the cosmic judge who punishes the wicked and maintains order.</note>

### Om. For Yama, the descendant of Angiras and the lord of the ancestors, Hail! Hail to the sacred heat of the offering! Hail to the sacred heat offered to the Ancestor!
<note>original: "oṃ yamāya tvāṅgirasvate pitṛmate svāhā | svāhā gharmmāya svāhā gharmmaḥ pitre ||" This Vedic mantra links Yama to the Angiras (a group of celestial seers) and the Pitris (ancestors). The word "Gharma" refers to the heat of the sacrificial vessel or the offering itself, signifying the transformative power of the ritual fire.</note>

### Om. Earth, Atmosphere, Heavens. O Yama, come here, stay here. Salutations to Yama; I invoke Yama and establish him here. || 3 ||
<note>original: "oṃ bhūrbhuvaḥ svaḥ yamehāgaccha iha tiṣṭha yamāya namaḥ, yamamāvāhayāmi sthāpayāmi || 3 ||" This is the standard installation formula used to invite the deity's presence into the ritual space, specifically into a designated pot or area on the altar.</note>

---

One should perform the <term>Avahana</term> (invocation) and <term>Sthapana</term> (establishment) of Yama by reciting the verse and mantra sentences starting from "I invoke Yama, mounted on a great buffalo..." until "...I invoke and establish Yama." || 3 ||

->I invoke the god Nirṛti, the lord of all departed spirits, for the success of the sacrifice;<-
->He who possesses a dark-blue body, is mounted upon a human, and is the granter of boons.<-
<note>original: "sarvapretādhipaṃ devaṃ nirṛtiṃ nīlavigraham | āvāhaye yajñasiddhyai narārūḍhaṃ varapradam ||" This verse provides the iconography for Nirṛti. While originally a goddess of destruction in the Vedas, in this directional ritual Nirṛti is personified as a male deity. His mount, a human (nara), represents the heavy burden of mortality or the suppression of the ego.</note>

### Om. Seek out the one who does not press the Soma juice, who does not sacrifice; follow the path of the thief and the robber. Seek someone other than us; that is your path. Salutations to you, O goddess Nirṛti.
<note>original: "oṃ asunvantamayajmānamiccha stenasyaityāmanvihi taskarasya | anyamasmadiccha sā ta ityā namo devi nirṛte tubhyamastu ||" This Vedic mantra is a plea to the personification of calamity and decay to bypass the current sacrificial site and its patrons, asking her to find those who do not honor the gods instead. Despite the male description in the previous verse, this ancient mantra retains the feminine address ("devi").</note>

### Om. Earth, Atmosphere, Heavens. O Nirṛti, come here, stay here. Salutations to Nirṛti; I invoke Nirṛti and establish him here. || 4 ||
<note>original: "oṃ bhūrbhuvaḥ svaḥ nirṛte ihāgaccha iha tiṣṭha nirṛtaye namaḥ, nirṛtimāvāhayāmi sthāpayāmi || 4 ||" This is the ritual formula to anchor the deity's presence into the sacred space.</note>

---

One should perform the <term>Avahana</term> (invocation), <term>Sthapana</term> (establishment), and worship of <term>Nirṛti</term> after reciting from the verse 'I invoke the god Nirṛti, the lord of all departed spirits...' and the <term>Mantra</term> 'Om. Seek out the one who does not press...' up to 'I invoke Nirṛti and establish him here.' || 4 ||
<note>The term <term>Nirṛti</term> refers to the guardian of the Southwest, often associated with destruction, sorrow, and the transition between life and death. <term>Avahana</term> is the ritual invitation for a deity to attend a ceremony, and <term>Sthapana</term> is the act of fixing their presence in a physical medium like a pot or an image.</note>

->**I invoke Varuna, the Lord of the West and the granter of all desires,**<-
->**Who resembles pure crystal, the Lord of Waters and master of aquatic creatures.**<-
<note>original: "śuddhasphaṭikasaṅkāśaṃ jaleśaṃ yādasāṃ patim | āvāhaye pratīcīśaṃ varuṇaṃ sarvakāmadam ||" This meditation verse (dhyana) provides the mental image for the practitioner. Here, Varuna is described as translucent and bright like crystal, emphasizing his celestial and pure nature as the sovereign of the cosmic waters.</note>

> Om. I come to you praying with the sacred word; the patron of the sacrifice desires that with offerings. Be mindful here, O Varuna, without anger; O wide-ruling one, do not steal away our lifespan.
<note>original: "oṃ tattvā yāmi brahmaṇā vandamānastadāśāste yajamāno havirbhiḥ | aheḍamāno varuṇeha bodhyuruśaꣳ sa mā naऽāyuḥ pramoṣīḥ ||" This is a famous verse from the Rigveda (1.24.11). It is a humble petition to Varuna—who in the oldest traditions was the judge of moral conduct—asking for his mercy, presence at the ritual, and the gift of long life.</note>

### Om. Earth, Atmosphere, Heavens. O Varuna, come here, stay here. Salutations to Varuna; I invoke Varuna and establish him here. || 5 ||
<note>original: "oṃ bhūrbhuvaḥ svaḥ varuṇa ihāgaccha iha tiṣṭha varuṇāya namaḥ, varuṇamāvāhayāmi sthāpayāmi || 5 ||" This is the standard liturgical formula to "anchor" the deity's energy into a physical representation, such as a water pot (kalasha) or a diagram (mandala).</note>

## I invoke Vayu, who is swift as the mind, endowed with great splendor, moving everywhere, and auspicious,
## For the purpose of protecting this sacrifice.
<note>original: "manojavaṃ mahātejaṃ sarvataścāriṇaṃ śubham | yajñasaṃrakṣaṇārthāya vāyumāvāhayāmyaham ||" This is a meditation verse (dhyana) used to visualize the deity. Vayu is characterized by his speed and his omnipresence, essential for guarding the ritual space from all sides.</note>

Om. O Vayu, come to our sacrifice with your teams of horses—by the hundreds and the thousands. Rejoice in this libation; and may you all protect us always with blessings.
<note>original: "oṃ ā no niyudbhiḥ śatinībhiradhvaraṃ sahasriṇībhirupayāhi yajñam | vāyo asminsavane mādayasva yūyaṃ pāta svastibhiḥ sadā naḥ ||" This Vedic mantra (Rigveda 7.92.3) invites the Wind God to descend and enjoy the offerings. The "teams of horses" (niyuta) symbolize the powerful gusts of wind that carry the deity.</note>

### Om. Earth, Atmosphere, Heavens. O Vayu, come here, stay here. Salutations to Vayu; I invoke Vayu and establish him here. || 6 ||

By uttering these words, the priest transitions from poetic invitation to the ritual reality of the god being present in the sacred vessel or diagram.</note>

## I establish Ananta, the lord of all serpents, who possesses the form of the universe;

# Establishment and Worship of the Countless Rudra-Vessels

Then, in the northeast <note>original: "ishana-digbhaga"</note> direction of the planets, having established the Rudra-vessel according to the procedure for establishing a ritual jar <term>kalasha|a sacred water pot representing the deity</term>, and having invoked Varuna <note>The Vedic god of the waters and moral order</note> and the Countless Rudras <note>original: "Asankhyata-Rudra"; the infinite, fierce manifestations of Shiva who protect the universe</note> into the jar, one should perform worship. It is as follows:

> Om. There are countless thousands of Rudras who dwell upon the earth.
> We unstring their bows a thousand leagues away.
<note>original: "oṃ asaṃkhyātā sahasrāṇi ye rudrā adhi bhūmyām | teṣāṃ sahasrayojane’va dhanvāni tanmasi |" This is a protection mantra from the Yajurveda (Shatarudriya) intended to appease the fierce Rudras by asking them to set down their weapons at a great distance from the worshiper.</note>

Salutations to the Countless Rudras; I invoke the Countless Rudras, I establish them.

> Om. May the mind's impulse enjoy the clarified butter; may Brihaspati <note>The priest and teacher of the gods</note> [expand] this sacrifice...

---

In the northeast corner of the planetary arrangement, establish the Rudra-vessel <term>Rudra-kalasha|a jar specifically consecrated to Shiva/Rudra</term> according to the ritual jar establishment procedure. Having invoked Varuna and the Countless Rudras into the vessel, perform the worship. The method is this:

After establishing the jar, recite from "Om. Countless thousands..." through to "I invoke and establish the Countless Rudras," and thereby call the Countless Rudras into that vessel. Then, taking consecrated rice <term>akshata|unbroken, colored rice grains used in ritual</term> in the right hand, by means of the mantra "Om. May the mind's impulse..."

# Performing the Kushakandika
<note>The Kushakandika is a foundational ritual involving the preparation of the sacred fire and the appointment of the Brahma priest, who supervises the ceremony to ensure no errors occur.</note>

To the south of the fire is the seat for the Brahma <term>priest</term>. To the north of the fire are two seats for the *Pranita* <note>holy water vessels used for purification</note>. The Brahma takes his seat at the Brahma-seat. The Patron <note>the person for whom the ritual is being performed</note> says: "Remain as the Brahma priest until this rite is completed." The Brahma should reply: "I shall so remain."

## Then, with the permission of the Brahma, the fetching of the *Pranita* water. It is as follows:

---

**Kushakandika**—After the establishment and worship of the Countless Rudras, one should perform the Kushakandika in this manner.

On a small wooden stool or a ritual platform, establish the seat of the Brahma to the south of the fire. To the north of the fire, place two blades of *Kusha* grass for the *Pranita* water vessel. At the Brahma’s station, tie a knot in fifty blades of *Kusha* grass and place them upon the Brahma’s seat. Then the Patron says this sentence to the Brahma: "Remain as the Brahma priest until this rite is completed." The Brahma likewise says, "I shall so remain."

After that, having received the Brahma’s permission, fill the *Pranita* vessel with water. The sequence is thus—taking the *Pranita* vessel in one’s own...

---

> <note>
> 1. The Brahma seat should be made of fifty blades [of grass], and the *Vishtara* <note>a ceremonial grass seat or bundle</note> of half that number. The Brahma's grass should have the tips pointing upward, while the *Vishtara* has tips hanging down.
> 
> The Brahma's seat is twisted to the right, and the *Vishtara* is twisted to the left. This is the characteristic described for the *Vishtara* in all sacrificial rites.
> <note>original Sanskrit: "pañcāśatā bhaved brahmā tadardhena tu viṣṭaraḥ | ūrdhvakeśo bhaved brahmā lambakeśastu viṣṭaraḥ || dakṣiṇāvarto brahmā ca vāmāvartastu viṣṭaraḥ | viṣṭaraṃ sarvayajñeṣu lakṣaṇaṃ parikīrtitam ||"</note>
> </note>

## Having placed the *Pranita* vessel <note>original: "pranitapatram"; a sacred vessel used to hold consecrated water</note> in front, filled it with water, and covered it with *Kusha* grass, one should place it on the first seat. Then, after looking at the face of the Brahma priest, place it on the second seat.

## The ritual spreading <note>original: "paristaranam"</note> of *Kusha* grass is done with the tips pointing East, beginning from the Northeast. Specifically: then, taking a fourth part of the *Barhi* <term>sacrificial grass bundle</term>, one should spread it from the Southeast to the Northeast with the tips pointing North; or from the Brahma’s station to the fire with the tips pointing East; from the Southwest to the Northwest with the tips pointing North; and from the fire to the *Pranita* vessel with the tips pointing East. Otherwise, the order is reversed.

<margin>

</margin>

---

Place it <note>the holy water vessel</note> in front, fill it with water, cover it with *Kusha* grass, and after placing that vessel on the first seat and looking at the face of the Brahma priest, place the *Pranita* vessel on the second seat.

After that, the "Kusha-gate" or ritual boundary: Perform the spreading of grass from the Southeast corner to the Northeast corner. It is done in this way—taking a fourth part of the *Barhi-Kusha* (a bundle of eighty-one, sixty-four, or a handful of *Kusha* grass is called *Barhi*) in the left hand, spread the grass with the right hand toward the North, from the Southeast corner to the Northeast corner. Then, with the tips of the grass pointing East, spread them from the Brahma’s seat to the sacrificial fire-pit; with the tips pointing North, spread them from the Southwest corner to the Northwest corner; and with the tips pointing East, spread them from the fire-pit to the *Pranita* vessel. Then, taking water in the hand, move it in a reverse circle.

<note>This ritual creates a "sacred fence" of grass around the fire to protect the sacrifice and define the ritual space.</note>

Taking up the three <term>fuel sticks</term> <note>original: "samidh"</note> anointed with clarified butter, one should cast them into the fire while standing. With the hand holding the <term>purifying grasses</term> <note>original: "pavitra"</note>, sprinkle water from the sprinkling vessel clockwise around the fire, starting from the northeast. Then, perform the same sprinkling in the opposite direction.

Place the two purifying grasses into the <term>consecrated water vessel</term> <note>original: "pranita"</note>. Bending the right knee and maintaining ritual contact with the <term>Brahman priest</term> <note>original: "brahmana"</note> through the <term>sacred grasses</term> <note>original: "anvarambha," the act of physical or symbolic connection during the offering</note>, perform the clarified butter offering with the small ladle into the most brightly burning part of the fire. 

In the northern part of the fire, recite: **"To the Lord of Procreation, Hail!"** <note>original: "Om Prajapataye Svaha"</note>. Then recite: **"This is for the Lord of Procreation, not for me."** In the southern part of the fire, recite: **"To Indra, Hail!"** <note>original: "Om Indraya Svaha"</note>.

---

While standing, cast the three fuel sticks into the fire. Again, with the hand holding the purifying grasses, move the right hand clockwise with the water from the <term>sprinkling vessel</term> <note>original: "prokshani"</note> from the northeast corner back to the northeast corner. In the same way, move the water vessel around the fire (the altar) in the opposite direction back to the northeast.

Afterward, place those two blades of <term>Kusha grass</term> into the consecrated water vessel. Bending the right knee and maintaining contact with the Brahman priest via the grasses, offer the clarified butter with the small ladle into the blazing fire. In the northern part of the fire—from "To the Lord of Procreation, Hail!" until "This is for the Lord of Procreation, not for me"—and in the southern part of the fire, "To Indra, Hail!"

---

> 1. When the ritual contact is made with the Brahman priest's right hand during the offering, one should stoke the fire with plenty of wood so that it is bright and capable of the ritual action.
> 2. In the nine ritual stages starting with the first, or in the eight types of clean actions, one should be connected to the priest; that contact is maintained specifically through the <term>sacred grass</term> <note>original: "kusha"</note>.
> 3. **Verse for holding the small ladle:** The wise one should hold the <term>small ladle</term> <note>original: "sruva"</note> from the middle of the tip, the middle of the center, and the middle of the base; this should always be known by the learned.
> During a ladle offering, the "relinquishment" <note>the mental dedication of the offering, called 'tyaga'</note> is always done over the sprinkling vessel. In offerings made by hand, this relinquishment is not required.

# **This is for Indra, not for me.** In the most brightly kindled fire—**Om, to Agni, Hail!** This is for Agni, not for me. **Om, to Soma, Hail!** This is for Soma, not for me.
# Then, for the Sun and other planets—including the <term>Presiding Deities</term> <note>original: "Adhidevata"</note>, the <term>Secondary Deities</term> <note>original: "Pratyadhidevata"</note>, the five <term>World Guardians</term> <note>original: "Panchalokapala"</note> such as Ganesha, the <term>Lord of the Dwelling</term> <note>original: "Vastoshpati"</note>, the <term>Guardian of the Field</term> <note>original: "Kshetrapala"</note>, and the ten <term>Directional Guardians</term> <note>original: "Dashadikpala"</note>—one should perform the sacrifice. For each deity, offer <term>fuel sticks</term>, sesame, <term>cooked grain</term>, and clarified butter 108, 28, or 8 times.

---

<margin>25</margin>
From the phrase "This is for Indra, not for me," and then into the freshly kindled fire, recite from "Om, to Agni, Hail!" to "This is for Soma, not for me" while making the offerings. At the conclusion, after saying "not for me" <note>original: "na mama"</note>, allow the remaining clarified butter from the <term>small ladle</term> <note>original: "sruva," used for small liquid offerings</note> to drip into the <term>sprinkling vessel</term> <note>original: "prokshani patra," a vessel used for ritual purification</note>.

Afterward, perform the <term>fire sacrifice</term> <note>original: "havan"</note> for the planets beginning with the Sun and ending with Ananta, the presiding and secondary deities, the five world guardians starting with Ganesha, the Lord of the Dwelling, the Guardian of the Field, and the ten directional guardians starting with Indra. The sacrifice should be made with <term>ritual fuel sticks</term> <note>original: "samidha"</note>, sesame, rice, and clarified butter—collectively referred to as the <term>sacrificial mash</term> <note>original: "charu"</note>. Offerings for each deity should be made either 108, 28, or 8 times.

<margin>286</margin>
1. Ark, Palash, Khadir, Apamarga, Pippal, Audumbar, Shami, Durva, and Kush are the nine types of ritual fuel. <note>These correspond to the nine planets: Sun, Moon, Mars, Mercury, Jupiter, Venus, Saturn, Rahu, and Ketu respectively.</note>
2. Regarding the proportions: It is said that rice should be half the amount of sesame, and barley should be half the amount of rice. Sugar should be half the amount of barley, and the clarified butter portion should be four parts.
(Or alternatively) It is said that rice should be half the amount of barley, and sesame should be half the amount of rice. Sugar should be half the amount of sesame, and the clarified butter portion should be four parts.

**The Ritual Resolution—** The <term>patron</term> <note>original: "Yajamana," the person sponsoring and benefiting from the ritual</note> taking water in his hand, shall state: “In this planetary peace ritual (or in the ritual named [Name of specific rite]), I relinquish these <term>offering materials</term> <note>original: "havaniya dravyani," the substances like grain or ghee to be burnt</note> for whichever deities are to be worshipped; they are not mine” <note>original: "na mama," a formulaic renunciation of the sacrifice's fruits</note>. Having spoken this, he should pour the water onto the ground. Then he should say, “May it be as the deities desire” <note>original: "yatha daivatani santu"</note>.

->**Thus ends the performance of the Kushakandika.**<-
<note>The Kushakandika is the essential preliminary ritual used to consecrate the sacred fire and prepare the altar before the main offerings begin.</note>

---

**Resolution—** Again, the patron, taking water in his right hand and reciting from “In this planetary peace ritual...” to “relinquished by me, it is not mine,” shall release the water onto the ground. He then speaks the phrase, “May it be as the deities desire.”

<margin>26</margin>

->In this way, the Kushakandika ritual is finished.<-

## Fire Offering to the Invoked Deities

Then, beginning with the mantra "Om, we invoke you, Lord of the hosts..." <note>original: "Om gananam tva..."</note> and continuing through to the mantra "Om, may the Earth be pleasant..." <note>original: "Om syona prithivi..."</note>, one should perform the fire offering with the <term>sacrificial materials</term> <note>original: "havaniya-dravya"; here specified as sesame seeds mixed with rice and clarified butter</note> for each individual mantra. It is performed as follows:

**Om! We invoke you, Lord of the celestial hosts <note>Ganesha</note>; we invoke you, Lord of those who are dear; we invoke you, Lord of the treasures! O my Lord of Wealth! May I be a vessel for the wisdom of the womb, and may you be the source of that wisdom. Hail! This offering is made. <note>original: "Svaha"</note> || 1 ||**

---

**The Fire Offering to the Invoked Deities —** Following this, recite each mantra starting from "Om, we invoke you, Lord of the hosts..." to the mantra "Om, may the Earth be pleasant...", and for each, offer the <term>charu</term> <note>a sacred mixture of cooked rice, clarified butter (ghee), and sesame seeds</note> into the consecrated fire for the deities who have been summoned to the ritual.

**Om! O Mother! O Dear Mother! Moving through the dark space <note>original: "krishna rajasa"; the dark regions of the sky before dawn</note>, establishing the immortal <note>gods</note> and the mortal <note>humans</note>, the divine Impeller <note>original: "Savita"; the sun deity who rouses the world</note> approaches on his golden chariot, beholding all the worlds. **Technical Vocabulary:**
*   **Hail! (Swaha):** The sacred word spoken to "seal" the offering.
*   **Om:** The primordial sound, used to begin most mantras.
*   **Fire (Agni):** The divine priest and messenger who takes the smoke of the sacrifice up to the gods.
*   **Thornless (Syona):** A prayer for the Earth to provide a smooth, safe, and comfortable life.
*   **Vishnu’s Strides:** A reference to the cosmic measurement of the world by the preserver god.
*   **Mantra:** A sacred chant or prayer used in ritual.
*   **Planets (Graha):** The celestial bodies whose influence is being harmonized by this ceremony.

# The Principal Fire-Offering <note>original: "Pradhāna-homaḥ"; the core part of the fire ritual dedicated to the main deity of the ceremony</note>

If the principal deity is **Vishnu**, then use the mantra: “Om! Through this, Vishnu [stepped]...” <note>original: "idam viṣṇuḥ"; referencing a Vedic verse describing Vishnu’s three steps through which he established the universe</note>. 

If it is **Shiva**, use the mantra: “Om! Salutations to your wrath, O Rudra...” <note>original: "namaste rudra"; the opening of the Shri Rudram, a prayer to Shiva in his fierce form</note>. 

For **Ambika** <note>the Divine Mother or Goddess</note>, use the mantra: “Om! O Mother, O dear Mother...” <note>original: "ambe 'ambike"</note>. 

Likewise, if **Ganapati** <note>Ganesha, the elephant-headed god who removes obstacles</note> or any other deity is the primary focus, then one should offer one hundred and eight oblations <note>original: "āhuti"; the act of pouring clarified butter (ghee) or grain into the sacred fire</note> using the specific mantras for those deities.

---

Principal Fire-Offering—If **Vishnu** is the primary deity, one makes offerings with the mantra “Om! This [is] Vishnu...”; if **Shiva** is primary, with the mantra “Om! Salutations to the wrath of Rudra...”; if **Ambika** (the Goddess) is primary, with the mantra “Om! Mother, Dear Mother...”; and if **Ganapati** or others are primary, one should offer one hundred and eight oblations with the specific mantras for those deities.

->This concludes the Principal Fire-Offering.<-

->-*-<-

**Key Ritual Terms:**
**Principal Fire-Offering** <note>original: "pradhānahoma"</note>, **Vishnu**, **Shiva**, **Ambika**, **Ganapati**, **Mantra** <note>sacred chant</note>, **Oblation** <note>original: "āhuti"</note>, **Fire-offering** <note>original: "havana"</note>

It prescribes the standard ritual count of 108 oblations for the primary deity.</summary>

# The Fire-Offering for the Deities of the Sarvatobhadra Mandala <note>A "Sarvatobhadra Mandala" is a sacred geometric grid or "yantra" used in Vedic rituals; it represents a celestial palace where various gods are invited to reside during the ceremony.</note>

Then, after the principal fire-offering <note>original: "pradhāna-homa"; the central part of the ceremony described on the previous page</note>, one should offer a single oblation <term>āhuti|the act of pouring an offering, usually clarified butter, into the sacred fire</term> of clarified butter <term>ghee|purified butter</term> to each of the deities within the Sarvatobhadra Mandala, starting with Brahma. This is done as follows: beginning with the mantra **“Salutations to Brahma, Svaha!”** <note>original: "Brahmaṇe namaḥ svāhā"; 'Svaha' is the sacred exclamation used when casting an offering into the fire</note> and continuing through to the final mantra **“Salutations to Vainayaki, Svaha!”** <note>Vainayaki is a female aspect of the deity Ganesha, who is often invoked at the conclusion of lists of deities</note>.

---

Fire-offering to the deities located in the Sarvatobhadra Mandala—Following the main fire-offering, one should offer one portion of clarified butter into the fire for each of the deities in the Sarvatobhadra Mandala, starting with Brahma. The procedure is as follows: recite from **“Salutations to Brahma, Svaha!”** to **“Salutations to Vainayaki, Svaha!”** while offering one oblation of clarified butter to each of the fifty-six deities <note>The Sarvatobhadra grid is traditionally populated by 56 specific deities who represent various cosmic forces and directions</note>.

->Thus ends the fire-offering to the deities of the Sarvatobhadra Mandala.<-

<header>Planet Procedures / The Svishṭakṛt Offering</header>

# The Svishṭakṛt Offering <note>The term "Svishṭakṛt" (literally "maker of the right sacrifice") is an epithet of Agni. This part of the ritual ensures that if any part of the complex ceremony was performed incorrectly, Agni will make it whole and acceptable to the gods.</note>

## The Worship of Fire. It is as follows:

> **"O Agni! Lead us by the good path to prosperity, O God, you who know all the ways. Remove from us the crooked sin; we offer you our most profound salutation."** <note>original Sanskrit: "Oṃ agne naya supathā rāye..." This is a famous Vedic prayer to the Fire God seeking guidance and purification.</note>

Using the mantra **"Om, salutations to Agni-Vaishvanara, who is joined with Svaha and Svadha!"** <note>original: "Oṃ svāhā-svadhāyutāgnaye vaiśvānarāya namaḥ"; 'Svaha' and 'Svadha' are the ritual exclamations used when offering into the fire for gods and ancestors, respectively. Vaishvanara is an epithet of Agni meaning "universal man" or "fire that belongs to all."</note> one should worship the fire with perfumes <note>usually sandalwood paste</note>, <term>akshata|unbroken grains of rice, often colored with turmeric or vermillion, used as a symbol of abundance</term>, flowers, and other ritual items.

->Thus ends the worship of fire.<-

---

The Svishṭakṛt Offering and the Worship of Fire—The <term>yajamana|the patron or host who commissions and pays for the ritual to be performed</term>, taking perfume, rice, and flowers in his right hand, should worship the blazing fire by reciting the mantras starting from **“O Agni! Lead us by the good path...”** through to the phrase **“...salutations to Vaishvanara.”**

->In this manner, the worship of fire is concluded.<-

# **Then, taking the remains of the sacrificial offering materials, and while being touched by the Brahman priest, one should perform the Svishṭakṛt offering.** <note>original Sanskrit: "tato hutaśeṣahavirdravyaṃ gṛhītvā...". In this ritual, the "Brahman" is the priest who sits in silence to supervise the ceremony. He touches the person performing the rite with sacred grass to create a spiritual connection and ensure the ritual's integrity.</note>
# **"Om! To Agni, the maker of the right sacrifice, Svaha! This is for Agni, the maker of the right sacrifice—it is not mine."** <note>original Sanskrit: "oṃ agnaye sviṣṭakṛte svāhā | idamagnaye sviṣṭakṛte na mama |". The phrase "na mama" (not mine) is a vital part of the ritual, symbolizing the renunciation of the offering and the ego.</note>
# **The casting of the remaining clarified butter into the vessel of sprinkling water.**

---

Thereafter, take the remaining <term>shakalya|a ritual mixture of grains, seeds, and herbs</term> (the <term>charu|sacred boiled rice oblation</term>). Touch the <term>Brahman|the overseeing priest</term> with <term>kusha|sacred grass</term>, and while reciting "Om, to Agni, the maker of the right sacrifice, Svaha!", cast the mixture into the fire. Then, saying "This is for Agni, the maker of the right sacrifice—it is not mine," one should cast the <term>ghee|clarified butter</term> remaining in the <term>sruva|the small wooden ladle used for pouring offerings</term> into the <term>prokshani-patra|the ritual vessel containing consecrated water</term>. <note>Mixing the remains of the fire-offering into the water vessel is a common concluding step, symbolically uniting the heat of the fire with the cooling properties of water.</note>

->In this manner, the Svishṭakṛt offering is completed.<-

## The Nine Oblations Starting with "Bhur" <note>original Sanskrit: Bhuradi-navahutayah. These are standard offerings made to the three spheres of existence—Earth, Atmosphere, and Heaven—along with specific prayers for divine grace.</note>

<margin>Planet Ritual Manual</margin>
Then, one should perform the nine oblations starting with the word "Bhur." As follows: **"Om, to the Earth, Svaha! This is for Agni—it is not mine." "Om, to the Atmosphere, Svaha! This is for Vayu—it is not mine." "Om, to the Heavens, Svaha! This is for Surya—it is not mine."** <note>The syllables Bhur, Bhuvah, and Svah represent the physical, mental, and spiritual planes. "Svaha" is the ritual exclamation used when casting an offering into the fire. "Na mama" (not mine) signifies the practitioner's surrender of the results of the deed.</note>

<margin>Nine Oblations</margin>
> **"Om! O Agni, you who are wise, appease the anger of the god Varuna. You, the most skilled sacrificer, the greatest bearer of offerings, radiant one—deliver us from all enmities. Svaha!"** <note>original Sanskrit: "oṃ tvaṃ no agne varuṇasya..." This is a Vedic prayer requesting Agni, the fire god, to act as an intermediary to calm Varuna, the stern guardian of cosmic law, and to remove any obstacles or ill-will.</note> **This is for Agni and Varuna—it is not mine.**

---

**The Nine Oblations Starting with "Bhur"** — Thereafter, taking <term>ghee|clarified butter</term> in the <term>sruva|the small wooden ladle used for pouring offerings</term>, one should offer the nine oblations into the <term>agni|the sacred fire</term> starting with "Om, to the Earth, Svaha!" It is performed as follows: reciting the sequence from "Om, to the Earth, Svaha!" up to "This is for Prajapati—it is not mine," one should offer the clarified butter with each <term>mantra|sacred chant</term> in succession. After saying "it is not mine" for each, let the remaining drops of clarified butter be dropped into the <term>prokshani-patra|the ritual vessel containing consecrated water</term>.

<note>This instruction clarifies that the practitioner must not only speak the words but also perform the physical act of "releasing" the remaining oil into the water vessel, symbolizing the completion of that specific portion of the rite.</note>

# The Offering of Food to the Ten Guardians of the Directions

->Around the sacrificial fire altar, in the four cardinal and four intermediate directions, as well as above and below, the offerings for the ten <term>Guardians of the Directions</term> <note>Sanskrit: Daśa-dikpāla; these are deities who preside over specific points of the compass, ensuring the ritual space is protected from all sides.</note> should be given. These offerings consist of lamps, yogurt, <term>black gram</term> <note>Sanskrit: Māṣa; a type of bean/lentil (Vigna mungo) used in rituals to appease powerful or potentially fierce deities.</note>, and cooked rice. They are offered as follows:<-

> **Om! Indra the Protector, Indra the Savior, whom we call in every invocation; Indra the Hero, the powerful one, I invoke Indra, who is called by many. May the generous Indra bestow well-being upon us.** <note>original Sanskrit: "oṃ trātāramindramavitāramindraṃ have have suhavaṃ śūramindram | hvayāmi śakraṃ puruhūtamindraṃ svasti no maghavā dhātvindraḥ ||" This is a traditional Vedic verse asking for the protection and favor of the king of the gods.</note>

->Having recited this mantra, one should say: "To Indra, along with his physical form, his retinue, his weapons, and his consort-power,<-
->I dedicate this offering of a lamp, yogurt, black gram, and cooked rice."<-

---

**Separate offerings for the ten Guardians of the Directions:** One should provide an offering to each of the invoked Guardians by placing a lamp on a leaf along with black gram mixed with yogurt and raw rice. The procedure is as follows: recite the mantra "Om! Indra the Protector..." and the sentence from "To Indra, with his limbs..." until the phrase "Be a granter of boons," and then place the leaf offering specifically for Indra.

<note>The text outlines a "Bali" ritual. Unlike "Homa" where offerings are burnt in fire, "Bali" involves placing food on the ground or on leaves for the deities and spirits to consume.</note>

<vocab>
**Ten Guardians (Daśadikpāla):** The deities of the eight compass points plus the zenith and nadir.
**Offering (Balidāna):** A gift of food, usually rice or grain, placed for deities or spirits.
**Indra:** The King of the Gods and guardian of the East.
**Mantra:** A sacred utterance or prayer.
**With Lamp (Sadīpa):** Accompanied by a small oil lamp or flame.
**Yogurt (Dadhi):** Used for its cooling and purifying properties.
**Black Gram (Māṣa):** A dark lentil often associated with protective or ancestral rites.
**Rice (Bhakta):** Specifically cooked rice in this context.
**Fire (Agni):** The sacred fire around which the ritual is organized.
</vocab>

# Ritual Offerings to the Planets

<margin>Planetary
Manual
321</margin> **To the Sun (Surya), along with his attendants, his family, his weapons, and his powers; together with the presiding and co-presiding deities <note>In Hindu planetary worship, each planet is associated with an Adhidevatā (presiding deity) and a Pratyadhidevatā (co-presiding deity). For the Sun, these are Ishvara (Shiva) and Agni (Fire).</note> in the forms of <term>Ishvara</term> and <term>Agni</term>—I dedicate this <term>offering</term> <note>Sanskrit: Bali; a ritual gift of food.</note> of rice and black gram mixed with curd, accompanied by a lamp. O Sun! Accept this offering; for me, my family, and my household, be the grantor of long life, the grantor of safety, the grantor of auspiciousness, the grantor of peace, the grantor of nourishment, the grantor of contentment, and the bestower of boons.**

<margin>Planetary
Offering
321</margin> **May the Sun be pleased by this act of offering. (1)**

**Om! O Gods, quicken this man to be without a rival, for mighty lordship, for mighty leadership, for mighty kingship over the people, for Indra's power of the senses. This man, the son of such-a-one...**
<note>original: "oṃ imaṃ devā asapatnaṃ suvadhvaṃ..." | This is a Vedic mantra from the Shukla Yajurveda (9.40) used during the consecration of kings (Rājasūya). In this liturgical context, it is used to invoke power and sovereignty for the practitioner through the Sun’s grace.</note>

---

Offerings to the planets and others—thereafter, in front of the <term>Planetary Altar</term> <note>Grahavedī; the sacred platform where the nine planets are symbolically installed.</note>, one should dedicate the offering of black gram and boiled rice mixed with yogurt, along with a lamp, to each of the planets.

One should present the offering to the Sun by reciting the mantra “Om! Returning through the dark...” <note>This refers to the Rig Vedic solar hymn "ā kṛṣṇena rajasā..." mentioned on the previous page.</note> and the liturgical passage starting from “To the Sun along with his attendants...” up until “be the bestower of boons.” Then, taking water in the hand and reciting the sentence “May the Sun be pleased by this offering,” one should release the water onto the ground. (1)

## Taking the offering, I dedicate these offerings—consisting of lamps, yogurt, and black gram rice—to the ten <term>Guardians of the Directions</term> <note>original: "daśadikpālebhyḥ" | These are the deities who preside over the eight compass points plus the zenith and nadir.</note> headed by Indra, including their various aspects, their entourages, their weapons, and their feminine powers.
<note>original: "sādīpa-dadhi-māṣa-bhaktabalīn" | Ritual food offerings (Bali) often use specific combinations; here, yogurt and black gram (māṣa) are used to appease and nourish the spirits and deities of the directions.</note>

## **The Prayer: O Indra and the other ten Guardians of the Directions, along with your aspects, attendants, weapons, and powers! For me and my family, be the creators of long life, the providers of safety, the makers of peace, the sources of nourishment, the givers of contentment, and the bestowers of boons.**

## **Then, taking water in the hand: "Through this offering, may the ten Guardians of the Directions headed by Indra be pleased." In this manner, one may present a single offering to all the planets through a unified rite.**
<note>original: "ekatantreṇa" | This refers to a "shorthand" ritual method where one ceremony suffices for multiple deities, saving time while maintaining efficacy.</note>

---

Having recited the mantra <term>"Om! To the Eastern direction, <term>Svāhā</term>!"</term> and said <term>"Salutations to the ten Guardians of the Directions led by Indra,"</term> one should worship the guardians with perfumes, consecrated rice, and flowers. Then, reciting the passage starting from <term>"To the ten guardians..."</term> until <term>"Be the bestowers of boons,"</term> one should offer a single, collective <term>offering</term> to the ten Guardians of the Directions accompanied by a prayer. Again, taking water in the hand and reciting the phrase <term>"By this offering..."</term>, one should pour the water onto the ground. In the same way, one may provide a single offering to all the planets through a unified ritual procedure.

->In this manner, the unified ritual offering to the ten directional guardians is concluded.<-

# Om! The planets, who bring vital strength, who are wandering and active, grant wisdom to the wise. Of those who are beloved and diverse, I have grasped the sap and the vigor. You are taken with a base; I take you as one pleasing to Indra. This is your source; I take you as most pleasing to Indra.

### Instructions for the Combined Offering

A single, unified offering <term>ekatantra</term> <note>A ritual method where one action or mantra suffices for a group of deities, rather than repeating the ritual nine separate times.</note> for the nine planets headed by the Sun: 

First, recite the aforementioned mantra: **"Om! The planets, who bring vital strength..."** Then, perform the worship of the nine planets (Sun, Moon, Mars, Mercury, Jupiter, Venus, Saturn, Rahu, and Ketu) using sandalwood paste, unbroken rice, flowers, and other items while saying **"Salutations to the Planets."** 

Next, recite the formal dedication sentence starting from **"To the nine planets headed by the Sun..."** and continuing until the phrase **"Be the bestowers of boons."**
<note>This refers to the prayer for protection and blessings found at the bottom of the previous page and the top of this one.</note>

I offer this sacrifice of curd, black gram, and cooked rice. <note>original: "dadhi-māṣa-bhakta-bali" | A traditional offering comprising yogurt, fermented beans, and boiled rice, intended to satisfy and appease the planetary spirits.</note>

**Prayer:** O Sun and the other planets! You who are accompanied by your various aspects, your retinues, your weapons, and your feminine powers; you who are joined by the primary presiding deities, the secondary presiding deities, the five World-Protectors headed by <term>Ganapati</term> <note>Ganesha, the elephant-headed god of beginnings.</note>, and the Lord of the Dwelling—for me, my family, and my household, please be the granters of long life, the granters of well-being, the granters of peace, the granters of nourishment, and the granters of satisfaction. May you be the givers of boons.

Again, taking water in the hand and saying, **"By this sacrifice, may the Sun and the other planets be pleased,"** one should pour the water onto the ground. <note>original: "anena balidānena sūryādigrahāḥ prīyantām" | The pouring of water symbolizes the finality and dedication of the ritual, "sealing" the offering to the deities.</note>

---

Having performed this, one should give a single, combined sacrifice to the Sun and the other <term>Navagrahas</term> <note>The Nine Planets: Sun, Moon, Mars, Mercury, Jupiter, Venus, Saturn, and the lunar nodes Rahu and Ketu.</note>. Then, taking water in the hand and reciting the sentence, **"By this sacrifice, may the Sun and the other planets be pleased,"** release the water onto the ground.

->In this manner, the collective sacrifice to the Sun and the other Nine Planets is concluded.<-

# Offering to the Guardian of the Field

In a single vessel made of bamboo or similar material, spread <term>Kusha</term> grass <note>Desmostachya bipinnata, a sacred grass used for purification and as a seat for deities in rituals.</note>. Upon it, place a food offering of <term>black gram, curd, and cooked rice</term> <note>original: "māṣa-dadhyodana" | This specific mixture is traditionally offered to protective or fierce spirits.</note> in a quantity that is either double or four times the amount of a standard human meal. Place a water vessel nearby, light a four-faced lamp <note>A lamp with four wicks facing the cardinal directions.</note>, and decorate the arrangement with turmeric, vermilion, and small banners.

<margin>Guardian Offering</margin>
> **Prayer:** Om. O Fire, the Universal Man! You are the observer of men; do not be ignorant of us. The immortals have nourished this immortal Fire, the Universal Man, so that the gods may be victorious over the fields. <note>This is a Vedic mantra (likely from the Shukla Yajurveda 15.60) invoking Agni as Vaishvanara to bless the land/field.</note>

One should then worship with the phrase **"Salutations to the Guardian of the Field"** <note>original: "kṣetrapālāya namaḥ"</note> using either the sixteen-fold or the five-fold sequence of offerings <note>original: "ṣoḍaśopacāra" or "pañcopacāra" | These are standard liturgical sequences ranging from simple (scent, flowers, incense, lamp, food) to elaborate (including bathing and clothing the deity).</note>. Then:

---

**Offering to the Guardian of the Field**—In a bamboo basket or on a double-layered leaf plate (spread Kusha grass and place upon it a human's) meal... <note>This final paragraph is a vernacular Hindi commentary repeating and clarifying the Sanskrit instructions above.</note>

## The Ritual Resolve for the Offering

The <term>Yajamana</term> <note>original: "yajamāna" | The patron or person for whom the ritual is being performed.</note>, taking water in his hand, [recites]:
> "To the Guardian of the Field <note>original: "kṣetrapāla" | A protective deity tasked with guarding a specific plot of land or sacred space.</note>, along with his physical form, his retinue, his weapons, and his power—and accompanied by the hosts of the goddess of death, the fierce Bhairavas, demons, gourd-spirits, corpse-spirits, ghosts, hungry ghosts, flesh-eating spirits, and the various classes of female spirits known as Dakinis, Shakinis, and Pishachinis <note>original: "mārīgaṇa-bhairava-rākṣasa-kūṣmāṇḍa-vetāla-bhūta-preta-piśāca-ḍākinī-śākinī-piśācinīgaṇa" | This list represents a wide array of supernatural beings in Hindu folklore that must be satisfied to ensure the safety of the site.</note>—I dedicate this offering of rice and black gram mixed with yogurt, presented along with a lamp."

Having uttered this, he should pour the water onto the ground.

### Prayer
> "O Guardian of the Field! Protect this field; consume this offering. For me, my family, and my kin, be the bringer of long life, the bringer of welfare, the bringer of peace, the bringer of nourishment, and the bringer of contentment. Be a granter of boons to us."

Having recited this, one should offer the formal prayer to the Guardian of the Field.

---

**The Ritual Resolve for the Offering** — The patron, taking water in his right hand and reciting the passage starting from “To the Guardian of the Field...” up to “I dedicate this offering of rice and black gram,” should pour the water onto the ground.

**The Prayer** — Next, having recited from “O Guardian of the Field, protect the field...” through to “Be a granter of boons,” one should pray to the Guardian of the Field.

<note>This final section provides a summary in the vernacular (Hindi) of the Sanskrit instructions above, ensuring the practitioner understands exactly which phrases to recite while pouring the ritual water.</note>

## The Final Oblation <note>Sanskrit: Pūrṇāhutiḥ; the "full offering" that concludes a Vedic sacrifice.</note>

Then, taking a coconut wrapped in red cloth and twelve, six, or four small ladlefuls <term>sruva|a small wooden spoon used to pour ghee into the larger ladle</term> of ghee <note>clarified butter</term> placed in the large ritual ladle <term>sruc|a large wooden pouring ladle used for major offerings</term>, and having placed the coconut upon it, one should worship it with the sixteen-fold offerings <note>ṣoḍaśopacāra; a standard sequence of sixteen acts of devotion including offering water, flowers, incense, and food</note> while reciting: **"Om, salutations to the Final Oblation."** Then, standing up, one should offer the final oblation into the fire:

> **Om. From the ocean, the honeyed wave has risen; together with the soma-stalk, it has reached immortality. The secret name of the ghee is the tongue of the gods and the navel of the immortal world.** <note>This is a translation of Rigveda 4.58.1, a famous hymn to Ghee (Ghrita) used during the final sacrifice.</note> **Let us proclaim the name of the ghee in this [sacrifice]...**

---

**The Final Oblation** — Thereafter, the patron <note>yajamāna; the person sponsoring the ritual</note> should remove the water from the coconut and fill it with ghee. He should then wrap that coconut in a red cloth. After pouring either twelve, six, or four small ladlefuls <note>sruvā</note> of ghee into the large ritual ladle <note>srucī-pātra</note>, he should place the coconut upon it, and then place the small ladle on top of the coconut. Having performed the worship of the coconut (representing the final oblation) with either the sixteen-fold or five-fold offerings while reciting the sentence: **"Om, salutations to the Final Oblation,"** he should stand up and begin reciting from **"Om, from the ocean, the honeyed wave..."** up to the concluding phrase **"Food and strength, O Lord of a hundred powers, Hail!"** <note>original: "īṣamūrjaṭh śatakrato svāhā"</note>.

<summary>This page describes the Purnahuti (Final Oblation) ritual, where a ghee-filled coconut wrapped in red cloth is offered into the sacred fire using ritual ladles to mark the completion of the ceremony.</summary>

O full ladle, fly away; well-filled, return to us. O Lord of a hundred powers <note>original: "shatakrato"; an epithet of Indra</note>, let us trade as if with a merchant, exchanging [offerings] for food and strength. **Svaha!** <term>Svaha|A sacred exclamation used when casting an offering into the consecrated fire</term> || 15 ||

### The Offering of the Flow of Wealth — Then one should perform the Vasordhara offering. As follows:

## Om, seven are your fuel-sticks, O Agni, seven your tongues, seven the sages...

---

After reciting the fifteen mantras ending here, one should offer the coconut into the blazing fire of the altar as the Final Oblation. In this manner, the <term>Purnahuti|The "Final Offering" that completes a major segment of a fire sacrifice, usually involving a whole coconut</term> is concluded.

# The Offering of the Full Vessel to the Brahma Priest

The patron <term>Yajamana|The person who sponsors and benefits from the ritual</term>, taking water in his hand, says: "As a required part of this completed fire-offering ceremony for the pacification of the planets, I offer this <term>Purnapatra|A 'full vessel,' usually a bowl filled with grain, cloth, or coins, symbolizing abundance and completion</term> along with the ritual fee to you, the <term>Brahma|The presiding priest who silently supervises the entire ritual to ensure no errors are made</term>." Having said this, he should pour the water onto the ground. <note>original: "कृतस्य ग्रहशान्तिहोमकर्मणोऽङ्गतया विहितमिदं पूर्णपात्रं स-दक्षिणं ब्रह्मणे तुभ्यमहं सम्प्रददे"</note>

"Om, may the Heavens give you; may the Earth receive you." <note>original: "ॐ द्यौस्त्वा ददातु पृथिवीत्वा प्रतिगृह्णातु"</note> Thus the Brahma priest should respond.

Following this, the release of the <term>Pranita|The vessel of sacred water placed to the north of the sacrificial fire at the start of the ritual</term> takes place behind the fire.

"Om, may the waters be auspicious, most auspicious, peaceful, and most peaceful; may they provide you with healing." <note>original: "ॐ आपः शिवाः शिवतमाः शान्ताः शान्ततमास्तास्ते कृण्वन्तु भेषजम्"</note>

One should then sprinkle and purify the area using the <term>Upayamana|The 'supporting' stalks of sacred grass used during the offerings</term> Kusha grass. This is followed by the casting of these supporting grass stalks into the fire. Finally, the untying of the <term>Brahmagranthi|The 'Knot of Brahma,' a specific ritual knot tied in the sacred grass strainers or the priest's seat</term> is performed.

---

The gift of the full vessel to the Brahma priest—The patron, taking water in the right hand, recites from the phrase "As a part of the completed..." to "...I give to you."

<margin>
**Ritual Vocabulary:**
*   **The Full Vessel Offering:** The final gift to the priest.
*   **Planetary Pacification:** The core purpose of this manual.
*   **Release of the Sacred Water:** Signaling the end of the water's ritual utility.
*   **Supporting Grass:** Used for handling and purification.
*   **Untying the Brahma-Knot:** Symbolizing the dissolution of the ritual's formal structure.
</margin>

<header>Manual for the Planets | Bestowing of Merit</header>

# Bestowing of Merit—The Preceptor
# Having recited the date and place, [the Preceptor says]: "I shall now perform the 'Bestowing of Merit' for the patron, resulting from this completed ceremony known as the Pacification of the Planets." 
# "By your appointment, whatever duties of the Preceptor I have performed in this ritual of Planet-Pacification (or in such-and-such ritual), I now hand over to you the spiritual merit arising from those acts, along with this water, grains of rice, and betel nut. 
# Please accept it." Thus the Preceptor should say. The patron responds, "I accept."

After reciting the <term>Sankalpa-vakya|The formal statement of intent that initiates a Hindu ritual</term>, he should release water onto the ground. The <term>Brahma|The priest who supervises the ritual in silence to correct any spiritual errors</term> priest should also recite the sentence: "Om, may the Heavens give you." <note>original: "ॐ द्यौस्त्वा ददातु"</note> Then, behind the sacrificial fire, one should turn over the <term>Pranita|The vessel of sanctified water placed north of the fire at the start of the rite</term> vessel and recite the prayer from "Om, may the waters be auspicious, most auspicious..." <note>original: "ॐ आपः शिवाः शिवतमाः"</note> until the word "healing." <note>original: "भेषजम्"</note> Using the water that has fallen on the ground, he should perform <term>Marjana|Ritual purification by sprinkling water</term> upon his own head using seven <term>Upayamana Kusha|Stalks of sacred Desmotachya bipinnata grass used to 'support' or hold the primary ritual offerings</term> grass stalks. Then, he should cast those supporting grass stalks into the fire and untie the knot of the <term>Brahma|Referring here to the 'Brahma-knot' or 'Brahmagranthi,' a specific sacred knot tied in the ritual grass</term>. With this, the donation of the <term>Purnapatra|The 'Full Vessel' symbolizing the completion and abundance of the rite</term> is concluded.

---

**The Bestowing of Merit**—Having recited the intention-statement from "On this day..." until "I shall perform the bestowing of merit," and from "By your appointment..." until "I hand over to you," and finally "Please accept," the Preceptor should bestow the merit (the credit for the fruits of the ritual performed thus far) upon the patron using a <term>Pugiphala|A betel nut, frequently used in Hindu rites as a physical representation of a deity or a spiritual value</term> (areca nut). The patron, saying "I accept," receives the merit.

It also details the final cleanup of the ritual space, including the purification of the head with sacred water and the burning of ritual grass.</summary>

5. To the **Overseer**: A conveyance carriage.
6. To the **Hotas** <note>The priests responsible for making offerings into the sacred fire</note>: Gold provided as <term>Dakshina</term>.

Thus should the Patron speak. The Brahma should respond, "May it be well." || 2 ||

### Concluding Worship of the Invoked Deities
Next, one should perform the concluding worship <note>original Sanskrit: 'uttara-pujana'</note> of the deities seated upon the planetary altar and other designated spots using the <term>Panchopachara|A standard five-fold offering consisting of scent/sandalwood paste, flowers, incense, a lamp, and food/water offerings</term>. The procedure is as follows: taking water in the hand, the patron makes the <term>Sankalpa|A formal statement of intent or ritual resolution</term>, saying: “For the sake of achieving the complete success of the performed Planet-Pacification ritual and to obtain its full fruit, I shall perform the concluding worship of the invoked deities.” After making this resolution, he should say: “Salutations to the deities invoked, beginning with Lord Ganesha <note>original: 'Ganapatyadi-avahita-devatabhyo namah'</note>.” Having uttered this, he should perform the five-fold concluding worship for the deities of the primary altar and the planetary altar.

# Giving the Main Altar and Other Items to the Preceptor

Then, the patron should give the main altar and other ritual items to the Preceptor <note>original Sanskrit: 'Acharya'</note>. The procedure is as follows: The <term>Yajamana|The patron or person commissioning the ritual</term>, taking water in his hand, recites: "For the sake of ensuring the completeness of this performed Planet-Pacification ritual <note>original Sanskrit: 'Graha-shanti-karman'</note> and to obtain its full intended fruit, I bestow this main altar, the planetary altar, the altar of the Mother Goddesses <note>original Sanskrit: 'Matrika-pitha'</note>, along with all the ritual equipment and the accompanying fees, to you, the Preceptor."

## The Consecratory Anointment

Then, after combining the water from the Rudra-vessel and the vessels of the other deities into a single container, the Preceptor and the four officiating priests <note>original Sanskrit: 'Ritvij'</note> should stand facing North. Holding <term>Durva|A sacred grass used in Hindu rituals for purification and as an offering</term> grass, Kusha grass, and the <term>Panchapallava|The 'five sprouts' or leaves from five sacred trees (usually Peepal, Gular, Pilkan, Bar, and Mango) used to sprinkle sanctified water</term>, they should anoint the patron and his wife, who are seated facing East with their family members to their North.

### The Ritual of Ghr̥tacchāyāpātradāna
<note>original: "घृतच्छायापात्रदानम्" (ghr̥ta-cchāyā-pātra-dānam); literally 'the giving of the vessel of the clarified butter reflection'</note>

"I, [Name] of the [Lineage] <term>Gotra|An ancestral clan lineage</term>—be I a Sharma, Varma, Gupta, or Dasa <note>The text provides options for the speaker’s surname based on their social class: Brahmin, Kshatriya, Vaishya, or Shudra respectively</note>—for the sake of successfully completing the ritual of <term>Graha-shanti|The pacification of the planetary deities</term> already performed, to obtain its full fruit, and for the destruction of all calamities, shall now perform the <term>Ajya-avekshanam|The ritual act of gazing into the sacrificial butter</term>."

Having made this resolution, he recites:

> Om. By your form, I have approached form. May the all-knowing <term>Tutha|A name for a divine priest or distributor of offerings</term> distribute you. Proceed along the path of Truth <note>original: "ऋतस्य पथा" (r̥tasya pathā)</note>. Behold the light of heaven with the moon as the sacrificial gift.

# "Spread through the mid-region along with the members of the assembly."
<note>original: "व्युन्तरिक्षं यतेस्व सदुस्यैः" (vyantarikṣaṃ yatesva sadusyaiḥ). This is a Vedic fragment used during the manipulation of ritual substances.</note>

<margin>Planetary Ritual</margin>
Having recited this <term>Mantra|A sacred Vedic verse or chant</term>, one should look at their own face reflected in the <term>Ghee|Clarified butter</term>.

The <term>Yajamana|The patron or person commissioning the ritual</term> should again take water in his hand and, after proclaiming the specific time and place, say: "I—[Name] of the [Lineage] <term>Gotra|An ancestral clan</term>, whether a Sharma, Varma, Gupta, or Dasa—give this clarified butter contained in a bronze vessel, along with a piece of gold, dedicated to the deity <term>Mrityunjaya|The 'Conqueror of Death,' a protective form of Lord Shiva</term>, to you, a well-worshiped <term>Brahmin|A member of the priestly class</term>, for the pleasure of Lord Mrityunjaya and for the destruction of all my calamities." 

Having recited this formal <term>Sankalpa|Sacred statement of intent</term>, he should hand the vessel of ghee to the Brahmin. 

<margin>Donation of Ghee</margin>
The Brahmin, upon receiving the vessel of ghee, should reply: "May it be well." <note>original: "स्वस्ति" (svasti)</note>

Taking water and reciting the formula from "Proclaiming the time and place" to "I shall perform the viewing of the ghee," one should then recite the mantra "By your form..." <note>Referencing the mantra on the previous page</note> and look at his reflection in the ghee.

Then, taking water in the hand again and reciting the formal declaration from "Proclaiming the time and place" to "I give this to you, the Brahmin," one should complete the donation.

> Whatever misfortune and whatever physical suffering has come upon my whole body;

# Vow for the Final Abundant Donation

One should give an abundant donation <note>original: "bhūyasīṃ dakṣiṇām"</note> to other <term>Brahmins|Members of the priestly class</term> according to one’s financial capacity. The <term>Yajamana|The patron or host of the ritual</term>, again taking water in his hand, should recite the following:

"For the successful completion of the constituent parts of this performed <term>Graha-shanti|Planetary peace-making ritual</term>, for the attainment of its full rewards, and to remedy any faults of deficiency or excess committed during the rite, I release this abundant donation to be distributed according to my means among the Brahmins of various names and lineages, my dependent kinsmen, and the poor and helpless."
<note>The "remedy of deficiency or excess" is a standard liturgical insurance policy, asking for the ritual to be considered perfect even if mistakes were made.</note>

Having pronounced this vow <note>original: "saṅkalpa"</note>, he should pour the water onto the ground and present the abundant donation to the Brahmins.

# In Praise of the Author

<margin>
Gra.
Pa.
377
</margin>
<margin>
Introduction
to the Work
377
</margin>

In the famous Deoria district, in a village named Majhaulika, where the world-renowned and mighty wrestlers once lived. || 1 ||

Where the <term>Brahmins|The priestly and scholarly class in traditional Indian society</term>—whose lotus-feet are worshipped by the entire world—became the ornaments of society, famous for their knowledge, good conduct, and success in spiritual practices intended for both this world and the next. || 2 ||

My grandfather was well-known to the world, named Shri Shrikanta, an expert in the secrets of the <term>Agamas|Sacred scriptures, often referring to those dealing with ritual, devotion, and Tantric philosophy</term>. He had two sons devoted to the highest truth, who were respected and possessed pure wealth <note>original: "achamva-rakta-vittau"; likely a reference to wealth earned through pure, righteous means</note>. || 3 ||

The elder was named Shri Sant Sharan, who was extremely famous, always engaged in the study of the scriptures and devoted to performing auspicious deeds. || 4 ||

The younger was named Shri Satya Narayan, who was blessed with good fortune. Both were devoted to their father and were highly skilled in serving the public. || 5 ||

The scholar Shri Sant Sharan had two sons who were full of devotion. The elder, Shri Jagannath, was a leader among the virtuous and was highly intelligent. || 6 ||

I am his younger brother, known by the name Shivadatta. I am devoted to serving my parents and take great pleasure in immersing myself in the ocean of the scriptures. || 7 ||

My first wife was named Vagishwari; she was the mother <note>original: "prasavitrika"</note> of my daughter Savitrika. My other wife was named Draupadi; though she gave birth to Pushpa <note>The author uses a play on words: "pushpa" means "flower," suggesting she blossomed through her child, or simply naming the daughter</note>, both have now attained liberation <note>This suggests both wives had passed away by the time of writing</note>. || 8 ||

My daughter Savitrika is a jewel among women; she is the wife of the wise Satyavrata, who is an expert in the arts and specialized knowledge of both the East and the West. || 9 ||

My younger daughter is Pushpa, the wife of the wise scholar Ramesharya. Both my daughters, having fulfilled their religious duties, are endowed with good fortune and prosperity. || 10 ||

I am an <term>Acharya|A title for a master teacher or scholar who has reached the highest level of traditional education</term> in Grammar <note>original: "shabda-shastra"; the science of words</note>, and I am constantly engaged in composing works in the ocean of literature. I have authored books on Tantra, hymns, grammar, and <term>Dharmashastra|The ancient Indian treatises on law, ethics, and social duty</term>. || 11 ||

To this day, over a hundred of my books have been published through great effort. I continue to work with tireless energy and perform the daily duties prescribed by the scriptures. || 12 ||

To satisfy the hearts of the refined and the faithful <note>original: "astika"; those who believe in the authority of the Vedas and the divine</note>, and having constantly studied a vast collection of scriptures, I have composed various treatises. I pray for the kind gaze of the wise upon these works. || 13 ||

-> ❈ ❈ ❈ <-

<meta>This page continues the instructional sequence for ritual preparation. # Now, the All-Auspicious Diagram
<note>original: "Sarvatobhadra Chakra"</note>

> One should draw nineteen lines moving from East to West, and nineteen lines moving from North to South <note>creating a grid of 324 squares</note>. The Crescent Moon <note>original: "Khandendu"</note> occupies three cells in each corner; the Chain <note>original: "Shrinkhala"</note> is formed with five cells. (1)

> The Vine <note>original: "Valli"</note> consists of eleven cells; the Auspicious Square <note>original: "Bhadra"</note> is made of nine cells. The Step-well <note>original: "Vapi"</note> comprises twenty-four cells, and the Perimeter <note>original: "Paridhi"</note> is formed of twenty cells. (2)

> In the center, within sixteen cells, an eight-petaled Lotus <note>original: "Padma"</note> is prescribed. One should fill the Crescent Moon with white, the Chain with black, and the Vine with blue. (4)

> The Auspicious Square is red, the Step-well is white, and the Perimeter is colored yellow. The outer and inner petals of the lotus are white, while the central seed-head <note>original: "Karnika"</note> is yellow. (3)

> The Lotus is enclosed by the Perimeter; outside of it are the three qualities of nature: Purity, Passion, and Inertia <note>original: "Sattva, Rajas, Tamas"</note>. In the center of this diagram, one should establish the deities, beginning with Brahma and the other lords of the gods. (5)

> If one is unable to perform worship using this complex diagram, one should create a simple, auspicious eight-petaled lotus. This should be made using wheat flour or, alternatively, with auspicious rice grains. (6)

<summary>This page provides the technical "blueprint" for the Sarvatobhadra Chakra, a complex 19x19 ritual grid. It details the specific cell counts for various geometric zones and the symbolic colors—white, black, blue, red, and yellow—required to empower the diagram for the invocation of Brahma and other deities.</summary>

<keywords>Sarvatobhadra Chakra, sacred geometry, ritual art, mandala construction, Gunas, Brahma, Vedic ritual, color symbolism</keywords>
