## Now, the All-Auspicious Diagram of the Four Lingams
<note>original: "Caturlingatobhadra Chakra"</note>

Eighteen lines are prescribed for the creation of the <term>Four-Lingam All-Auspicious Diagram<note>a complex ritual grid used in Hindu ceremonies, specifically dedicated to Shiva</note></term>. In each corner, the Crescent Moon <note>original: "Indu"</note> consists of three squares and is white; the Chain <note>original: "Shrinkhala"</note> is also formed of three squares and colored black. (1)

The Vine <note>original: "Valli"</note> consists of seven squares and is blue; the Auspicious Square <note>original: "Bhadra"</note> is red and made of four squares. Beside the Auspicious Square is the Great Rudra <note>original: "Maharudra," a fierce form of Shiva</note>, which is colored black and occupies eighteen squares. (2)

Beside the Shiva-space, one should create a white Step-well <note>original: "Vapi"</note> of five squares. A single square, colored yellow, should be placed in the middle, between the Auspicious Square and the Step-well. (3)

At the head of the Chain, one should place three yellow squares. Moving from the "shoulders" of the Lingams, twenty squares are to be colored red. (4)

The Perimeter <note>original: "Paridhi"</note> is recorded as having sixteen yellow squares. Finally, with nine squares, one should create a red Lotus <note>original: "Padma"</note> complete with its central seed-head <note>original: "Karnika"</note>. (5)

<summary>This page provides the precise geometric and color-coded instructions for constructing the Caturlingatobhadra Chakra, a specialized ritual mandala featuring four Lingams dedicated to the god Shiva.</summary>
<keywords>Caturlingatobhadra Chakra, Mandala, Shiva, Lingam, ritual geometry, Maharudra, Vapi, Valli</keywords>

## Now, the Form of the Fire Pit
<note>original: "Ath Kundasvarupam"</note>

The <term>Receptacle<note>original: "Yoni"; a specific heart-shaped structure or projection on the side of the fire pit that symbolizes the creative source from which the sacred fire is born</note></term> is 12 <term>finger-breadths<note>original: "Angul"; an ancient Indian unit of measurement based on the width of a finger, roughly 1.75 cm or 0.75 inches</note></term> high, 12 finger-breadths long, and 8 finger-breadths wide; it is red in color.

The white upper <term>step<note>original: "seedhi," technically referred to in ritual texts as a "mekhala"</note></term> is 4 finger-breadths wide and 4 finger-breadths high. (1)

The red step below that is 3 finger-breadths wide and 3 finger-breadths high. (2)

The black step below that is 2 finger-breadths wide and 2 finger-breadths high. (3)

---

<note>The text describes the construction of the tiered boundary of a sacrificial altar. The accompanying diagram indicates the cardinal directions: East at the top, West at the bottom, North on the left, and South on the right. The colors white, red, and black are symbolically significant in Hindu ritual, often representing the three fundamental qualities of nature: purity, activity, and stability.</note>

<summary>This page provides the precise measurements and color-coding for the tiered steps (mekhalas) and the heart-shaped receptacle (yoni) of a ritual fire pit. It serves as a technical guide for the physical construction of an altar used in fire sacrifices.</summary>
<keywords>Kunda, ritual fire pit, Yoni, Angul, finger-breadth, Mekhala, sacred geometry, Vedic ritual, altar construction</keywords>

# Now, the Diagram of the Nine Planets
<note>original: "Ath Navagrahacakram"</note>

Venus and the Sun should be known as facing East;
Jupiter and Mercury as facing North. Saturn and the Moon
face West; the rest face towards the South. (1)
<note>The "rest" refers to Mars, Rahu, and Ketu.</note>

All of them, along with their <term>presiding and sub-presiding deities<note>original: "Sadh-pratyadhidevatah"; in Hindu ritual, each planet is accompanied by a primary deity (Adhidevata) and a secondary deity (Pratyadhidevata) who govern its energy</note></term>,
should be established, O best of sages, facing the Sun,
and not facing away from one another. (2)
<margin>North</margin>

— **Thus it is stated in the Skanda Purana.**
<note>The Skanda Purana is one of the eighteen major Puranas (ancient religious texts) and is the largest, often focusing on the mythology and rituals associated with the god Kartikeya.</note>

<margin>East</margin>
| | | |
|:---|:---:|---:|
| <term>Mercury<note>original: "Budha"</note></term> | <term>Venus<note>original: "Shukra"</note></term> | <term>Moon<note>original: "Chandra"</note></term> |
| <term>Jupiter<note>original: "Guru"</note></term> | <term>Sun<note>original: "Surya"</note></term> | <term>Mars<note>original: "Bhauma"</note></term> |
| <term>Ketu<note>original: "Ketu"; the South Lunar Node</note></term> | <term>Saturn<note>original: "Shani"</note></term> | <term>Rahu<note>original: "Rahu"; the North Lunar Node</note></term> |
<margin>South</margin>
<margin>West</margin>

<note>This diagram represents the standard layout for the Nine Planets (Navagraha) used in Vedic astrology and ritual. The Sun occupies the central position, reflecting its role as the center of the celestial order, while the other eight entities—including the nodes of the moon, Rahu and Ketu—are arranged in the surrounding squares. The placement follows a specific geometric and directional logic intended to harmonize planetary influences during a ceremony.</note>

<summary>This page provides instructions from the Skanda Purana on the orientation and placement of the nine planetary deities within a ritual diagram. It includes a 3x3 grid (chakra) showing the Sun at the center, surrounded by the other eight planetary figures.</summary>

# The Hymn of Light for the Blessed Lord of the Universe <note>original: "Bhagavān Śrījagadīśvarkī Āratī"</note>

<margin>
Planets <note>original: "Graha." abbreviation</note>
Page <note>original: "Pa." abbreviation</note>
363
</margin>

> Om! Victory to the Lord of the Universe, Lord, victory to the Lord of the Universe! <note>original: "Om jaya jagadīśa hare." This is the opening of a famous hymn composed by Shardha Ram Phillauri in the 1870s.</note> You remove the troubles of your devotees in a single moment. || 1 ||
>
> Whoever meditates [upon Him] obtains the fruit; the sorrows of the mind vanish. Lord! Wealth and prosperity enter the home, and the sufferings of the body are erased. || 2 ||
>
> You are my mother and my father; whose refuge should I seek? Lord! Beside You, there is no other for whom I could hope. || 3 ||
>
> You are the Perfect Supreme Soul, You are the Inner Dweller <note><term>Antaryāmī</term>: the one who dwells within the heart and knows all thoughts.</note>. Lord! You are the Supreme Brahman, the Supreme Lord, the Master of everyone. || 4 ||
>
> You are the ocean of compassion, You are the sustainer. Lord! I am a foolish, wicked, and lustful man; O Provider, show mercy! || 5 ||
>
> You are the one beyond the reach of the senses <note><term>Agochara</term>: that which cannot be perceived by the eyes or physical senses.</note>, the Lord of the life-breath of all. Lord! By what method shall I meet You, O Merciful One? I am of poor intellect. || 6 ||
>
> Friend of the lowly, remover of sorrow, You are my protector. Lord! Lift Your hand of compassion; I have fallen at Your feet for refuge. || 7 ||
>
> Eliminate my worldly attachments and flaws, take away my sins, O Divine One. Lord! Increase my faith and devotion, and my service to the saints. || 8 ||

<summary>This page presents the lyrics to the "Om Jai Jagdish Hare" Aarti, a central devotional hymn in Hindu worship used to conclude rituals and express total surrender to the Divine. It emphasizes the Lord's role as a protector, sustainer, and the inner soul of all beings.</summary>
